PREFACE 
I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this One Hundred Twenty First  Report of the Committee on Action Taken by 
Government on the Recommendations/ Observations contained in One Hundred Tenth Report on 
Functioning of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India.  
2. The One Hundred Tenth Report of the Department -related Par liamentary Standing 
Committee on Health and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of 
Lok Sabha on 9 th August, 2018. Action Taken Note of the Government on the recommendations 
contained in the Report was received from the Ministr y on 4th February, 2019 .  Two sets of 
questionnaires on the ATN were forwarded to the Department of Health & Family Welfare and 
the Department furnished the replies thereto on 20th June, 2019 and 5th June, 2020 respectively.  
3.  The Committee has noted that the statement on the status of implementation of the 
recommendations contained in the said Report of the Committee has not been laid on the Table of 
Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha in pursuant to the direction of Chairman, Rajya Sabh a dated 24th 
September, 2004. 
4. The Committee made a total o f 126 recommendations in its 110 th Report.  Out of the 12 6 
recommendations, a total number of 40  recommendations have been accepted by the Ministry, 
has been categorized under Chapter I and there  are a total number of 33 recommendations, which 
the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Ministry’s replies,  has been categorized 
under Chapter II.  A total number of 46 recommendations/ observations in respect of which 
replies of the Minis try have not been accepted by the Committee and the Committee has made 
further recommendations thereon, has been categorized under Chapter III while a total number of 
7 recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not  been 
received, has been categorized under Chapter IV.   
5. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 
the 7th September, 2020.

CHAPTER–I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 It has been given to understand that FSSAI is presently operating with staff from 
state apparatus.  The Committee opines that FSSAI cannot function to its optimum level 
without employing technical persons as permanent staff.  The Committee recommends that 
FSSAI should be restructured and persons with domain knowledge and expertise in the food 
sector should be employed to run organization.  
 
1.2 The Committee notes the shortcomings pointed out in CAG report about the 
administration of food safety laws.  The Committee opines that there is a need to restructure 
or revamp the FSSAI so as to enable it to meet the multiple challenges in the arena of food 
safety and regulation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that only technically 
competent officers with exper tise in subject of food science should be appointed/ selected in 
FSSAI so that they are most suitable for the task assigned to them by FSS Act 2006. 
(Para 1.20 & 1.53) 
Action Taken 
 
1.3 The Ministry submitted that the Recruitment Regulations notified on 1s t October 
2018 and the posts sanctioned at various levels by Government are based on the 
organizational restructuring of FSSAI.  The mandate of FSSAI under the Food Safety and 
Standards Act, 2006 is to ensure safe and wholesome food for human consumption. This 
overarching mandate calls for action on traditional regulatory functions (setting standards, 
regulations, enforcement, food testing, risk management, research etc.), combined with the 
need for capacity building and consumer empowerment.  Accordingly, the Recruitment 
Regulations have 3 broad categories of posts to fulfill the mandate viz. Scientific and 
Technical posts (that constitute the bulk of the posts): IT and Specialized Services (including 
inter-alia training and capacity building, social and be havioural change communication etc.) 
and Support Services. Hence, the structure of the organization has been carefully created to 
ensure that the varied nature of its functions are handled effectively. 
 
1.4 The Ministry also submitted the following details: 
 
 135 posts have been re -designated at various levels as per details at Annexure 1.This 
re-designation reflects the enhanced job description in the light of evolving functions 
of the Authority, and also the merging of numerous fragmented cadres and sub -cadres 
into 3 major groups as brought out above, for smoother administration and better 
career growth prospects. 
 Of the 824 posts sanctioned, 415 posts have been advertised at various levels in the 
first phase of recruitment. Almost 1.6 lakhs applications ha ve been received against 
the advertised posts and a robust selection procedure, comprising of a Computer 
Based Test, Written Examination and Interview (as applicable) is in place. The exams 
are scheduled in July 2019 and September/October 2019.  The second  phase of 
recruitment will be taken up after the completion of the first phase, with the aim to 
complete the recruitment process within a period of 2 years.  
 The contractual employees have been given weightage  in selection and have an 
opportunity to appear and qualify through the selection process. Further, since the 

2 
 
process of recruitment is being taken up in phases, contractual employees would have 
more than 1 opportunity to prepare and participate in the selection process 
 
1.5 The Ministry further submitted that the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India 
(FSSAI) has advertised a total 307 vacancies at various levels in Phase -I of recruitment 
process vide Advt. No. DR-01/2019, DR-02/2019 & DR-03/2019. 
  
1.6 The recruitment process for 04 posts of Director and 06 posts of Food Analyst 
advertised against Advt. No. Dr-01/2019 and DR-03/2019 has been completed. Against these 
posts,  of the selected persons, 3 are contractual employees of FSSAI.   Selection pr ocess for 
other posts is going on and is likely to be completed by end of this year. Second phase of 
recruitment will be started thereafter. All vacant posts will be included in the second phase of 
recruitment. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.7 The Committee notes that as per the information available on the website of FSSAI, 
out of its 9 members of Central Advisory Committee (CAC) representing the interests of food 
industry, agriculture, consumers relevant research bodies and food laboratories, 5 are from 
Delhi.  The ex -officio Chairman of CAC is also Delhi based which makes this number six.  
Given the fact that there are 24 chapters under trade laws dealing with food and scope of 
FSSAI and there is vast pool of expertise available country -wide, this Delhi cen tric 
composition of CAC hardly represent various interest groups.  The Committee feels that this 
factor is certainly depriving FSSAI of the sage advice and expertise of the immense talent 
present in the food sector in the country.  This also leads the Committee to the conclusion that 
there is no transparent procedure for selection of members of CAC.   
1.8 The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be written guidelines on the 
selection process of members of CAC and the whole selection criteria s hould be made 
transparent.  Bio data of selected candidates and their areas on competency/proven track 
record should be displayed on the website of FSSAI.  It also recommends that the 
composition of CAC be broad based so that the pool of expertise in the f ood sector spread 
across the country could be tapped. 
(Para 1.25 & 1.26) 
Action Taken 
1.9 The recommendations of the Committee have been accepted and a transparent 
procedure for selection of members of CAC has been initiated. 
Recommendation /Observation 
 
1.10 The Committee observes that the responsibility for surveillance and enforcement of 
food laws lies squarely on the State/UT Governments.  But given the resource crunch in the 
States, it would be unrealistic to expect that the States would be in a positi on to improve the 
infrastructure and increase the manpower without central assistance for overhauling their 
food regulatory system. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Health 
and Family Welfare should work out a fully Centrally Sponso red Scheme for up-gradation of 
manpower, strengthening of food safety infrastructure including food testing laboratories and 
setting up a robust surveillance system at State level.  
(Para 1.42) 
 
 

3 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.11 On the Committees recommendations for a fully Centrally Sponsored Scheme for 
upgrading manpower, strengthening infrastructure and robust surveillance systems at the state 
level, it is submitted that FSSAI is implementing a Central Sector Scheme for strengthening 
of food testing laboratories and upgrading manpower. 37  State Food Laboratories of 29 
States/UTs have been upgraded and grants of Rs.220.30 crores  released. 43 mobile food -
testing vans called Food Safety on Wheels (FSW) have been delivered to 31 States/UTs. For 
upgradation of manpower, FSSAI has created centralized content and trainers for regulatory 
staff of States/UTs, which has been uniformly adopted. Further, 1500 lab personnel have 
been trained. Regarding hiring of manpower, while States/UTs sanction posts at the state 
level, centra l government has recently sanctioned 824 posts for FSSAI. To increase the 
manpower at State level, FSSAI has been taking up the issue of need for adequate manpower 
at various platforms with States/UTs. Several States namely, Gujarat, Chattisgarh, Manipur, 
Tripura, Nagaland, West Bengal, Meghalaya, Goa, Maharashtra and Jharkhand have already 
proceeded in this regard and recruited full time DOs and FSOs. The number of FSOs and 
DOs has gone up from 2324 and 630 in 2015 to 3373 and 741 in 2019, respectively. 
1.12 Other issues such as a robust surveillance system at the State level are being 
addressed through use of a common IT platform across States/UTs and setting of uniform 
checklists. 
 
Recommendation /Observation 
 
1.13 The Committee would like the Ministry to  launch a national level awareness 
programme to sensitize all the sections of the society on the food safety subject aiming to 
infuse a national commitment towards reduction of food contamination from all the stages of 
food chain.  This sort of a mission m ode project will assure that the stakeholders take full 
ownership and responsibility and ensure self -compliance of the FSS Act, 2006.  Also, a 
comprehensive food policy must be devised and the shortcomings of the present Act need to 
be rectified.   
(Para 1.54) 
Action Taken 
1.14 The Eat Right India Movement, aligned with the Government of India’s focus on 
public health through its three key programs ‘Ayushman Bharat’, ‘Swachh Bharat Mission’ 
and ‘Poshan Abhiyan, centres around the key themes of eat safe and eat healthy. The 
Movement and other social and behavioural change initiatives of FSSAI have witnessed 
enthusiastic engagement and keen participation from all stakeholders. Eat Right India aims at 
a 360 0 approach for citizen guidance and behavioural change through Safe and Nutritious 
Food (SNF) everywhere - at home, workplace, school. Resource books developed for Home 
(Pink Book) and Schools (Yellow Books) have been disseminated widely, both through print 
and electronic media;7000+schools have enrolled and c onducted 11000+ activities to 
promote healthy eating among students; 75000+ children participated in the Eat Right 
Creativity Challenge; Mascots Master and Miss Sehat have touched 1.5 million people, 
mostly schoolchildren. Simultaneously, food businesses h ave participated enthusiastically in 
the Food Safety Training and Certification (FoSTaC) initiative, with over 1.5 lakh Food 
Safety Supervisors trained through 160 training partners across 35 States/UTs through 5400+ 
training programs. Programs such as Cle an Street Food Hub have been adopted in 13 states, 
while Hygiene Rating, a certification Scheme for Restaurants/Caterers has completed 600+ 
audits. In a unique outreach initiative, aPan-India cycle rally, Swasth Bharat Yatra launched 

4 
 
on 16th October 2018, to spread the message of Eat Right India mobilised 21,000+ volunteer 
cyclists, covered over 20,000 kms and touched 2100+ locations in 100+ days, reaching out 
to2.5 crore people.Its biggest benefit has been in terms of re -energising States, food 
businesses and professionals, who are working at their level to take the movement forward.  
1.15 While the results so far have been encouraging, most of these initiatives are still in 
their nascent stages. Any behavioural change initiative takes decades of sustained effort to 
show noticeable changes in habits and culture. Hence, FSSAI envisions the Eat Right 
Movement as one that grows organically as a self -perpetuating movement, co-owned and co-
led by various partners, using the broad framework and resources put together. 
1.16 The mandate of FSSAI derives from the framework of the legislation viz. the Food 
Safety and Standards Act 2006, and various policies and initiatives of FSSAI are framed and 
undertaken within this legislative framework. Accordingly, to fulfil the broad mandate of 
ensuring safe food for all citizens of the country, and also enable food businesses in 
complying with various provisions within the scope of the Act, FSSAI has taken several steps 
like easing of food imports, adoption of ingredients based approach to standards and 
simplification of process of registration and licensing. Further, as advised by the Committee, 
to address shortcomings in the present Act and thereby ensure a comprehensive food policy, 
some  amendments in the FSS Act have been pr oposed to plug gaps and in furtherance of 
fulfilment of objectives of the Act which include inter alia: bringing ‘Animal Feed’ within the 
ambit of FSS Act to enable FSSAI to monitor inputs such as pesticides and veterinary drugs 
used by producers of animal  farm products; provision of deterrent punishment in case of 
unsafe food if it has potential to cause death or grievous hurt; provision of Reference 
Laboratories for the purpose of method development, method validation etc.; and including 
exports within the ambit of FSS Act. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.17 Considering all the facts, the Committee is constrained to observe that though the 
Supreme Court struck down the Product Approval System based on the advisories issued by 
FSSAI in August 2015, FSSAI took a very long time to review all the cases of NOCs gra nted 
under this system.  The status of 192 NOCs is still not clear as to whether these products are 
covered under any new regulations or not.  The Committee endorses the view of CAG that 
FSSAI failed to ensure the cancellation of licenses issued under this  suspended system.  
There is every likelihood that FBOs with invalid licenses under this system are still producing 
and selling unsafe food to the consumers. FSSAI should therefore expedite the whole process 
of withdrawal of such NOCs and carry out within six months’ inspection of the FBOs that 
claim to comply with the new regulations.  
(Para 2.12) 
Action Taken 
1.18 An order was issued on 1 st January, 2018 where all the 212 NOC holders were 
advised to confirm whether their products were in complete complian ce with the 
requirements of the regulations under which they now stand covered and also to get their 
licenses re-issued as per the appropriate category. Out of these, 8 NOC holders requested for 
re-examination of their NOCs as per the Non Specified Food Re gulations, 2017. 
Subsequently the remaining 204 NOCs issued were withdrawn on 27 th September 2018 under 
intimation to the Central Designated Officers and Authorized Officers. 
1.19 It was decided to carry out inspection in respect of   NOC cases in which lic ence was 
held  which related to 37 FBOs. The Central Licensing Authorities of FSSAI arranged for 

5 
 
inspection of all 37 units. Out of these 37 cases, 27 FBOs applied for modification in their 
license, 3 FBOs’ license have since expired, 6 FBOs were found to be compliant and 1 FBO’s 
license was cancelled. 
 
Recommendation /Observation 
1.20 The Committee notes that the first objective of FSSAI,  is to lay down science based 
standards for articles of food and regulate their manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and 
import to ensure availability of safe and wholesome food. However, the indicators of food 
safety show that the objective of formati on of FSSAI has not been fulfilled as the quality of 
food stuffs is deteriorating and use of contaminants is increasing day by day.  Milk and food 
which were safe previously are no longer safe because adulteration and use of hazardous 
chemicals for artificial ripening of fruits and vegetables have witnessed tremendous increase 
in the recent past.  The Committee observes that FSSAI has failed to assess the impact of the 
FSS Act on food safety and therefore recommends that FSSAI should systematically evaluate  
the performance of the FSS Act, its rules and regulations.  Certain indicators need to be 
developed to measure the outcomes of the food safety policy and institutions.  
(Para 2.3) 
Action Taken 
 
1.21 Recommendations of the Standing Committee have been note d and in its compliance 
action has been initiated to develop indicators needed to measure the outcomes of the food 
safety policy and institutions. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.22 The Committee notes with concern that many of the harmful components and 
contaminants enter the food system at the time of primary production whereas such primary 
food production is exempted from the coverage of the law.  The Committee believes that this 
exclusion of the farmer/fisherman or farming operations including fisheries, livestock from 
FSS Act is a major challenge and lacuna in the Act because unless the raw material is of good 
quality, the good quality of final product cannot be ensured.  The Committee agrees that it is 
important to ensure that the food is safe right from  the beginning of the food chain and for 
this, the Food Authority will have to work closely with the primary producers.  The major 
issues in primary production like overuse of pesticides, use of growth hormones, drug use in 
livestock etc. pose health risks  and a significant threat to ensuring food safety.  The 
Committee is convinced that without primary production system coverage, food will never be 
safe.  The Committee is aware that once hazardous contaminants, excessive antibiotics 
residues and pesticides  etc. enter the food system, there is no technology by which they can 
be removed from the foods.  The Committee, therefore, expects the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare to make guidelines/code of practices and the Ministry of Agriculture to 
impose res trictions on pesticides and harmful components.  The issue of amendment to 
necessary guidelines/code of practices may be taken up with the highest authorities 
concerned.  
(Para 2.30) 
Action Taken 
1.23 This Ministry entirely endorses the concern about issue s of food safety arising from 
exclusion of primary production from the ambit of the FSS Act, 2006. In many countries, 
around the world, counterpart food safety authorities are responsible for plant health, animal 

6 
 
health. There is particular focus on risk a rising from unsafe animal feed, plant protection 
products and veterinary drugs including antibiotics under the overall concept of ‘One Health’.  
 1.24 Sub clause (i a) is proposed to be added in Section 3 (1) of FSS Act to define the 
‘feed’ as under: 
3 (1) (ia) “Feed” means any substance which is ground pelleted or crumbled, 
contain source of energy and tissue building constituents like carbohydrates, 
protein, fat, minerals etc. which will provide all of the nutritional requirements 
necessary for the mainte nance of life or for promoting production of food 
producing animals including feed additives, various products of vegetable or 
animal origin, in their natural state, fresh or preserved, compound feed, 
medicated feed, genetically modified feed and products derived from the 
industrial processing thereof, and organic or inorganic substances, whether or 
not containing additives, which are intended for use in the preparation of 
compound feeding stuffs or as carriers of pre -mixtures. It does not include 
veterinary medicinal products and water. 
1.25 A proviso has been proposed to be added in Section 18 (3) of the FSS Act which 
reads as under: 
Provided that the producers of animal farm products shall apply inputs such as 
pesticides and veterinary drugs and adopt suc h practices that does not

1.46 The views of the Committee have been agreed to. FSSAI has examined the feasibility 
of granting license/registration on permanent basis. Apart from its revenue implications, there 
are a few other difficulties in granting permane nt license. At the time of renewal of license, 
presently the food businesses are required to provide details of the technically qualified 
person in charge of operations as well as the person responsible for complying with 
conditions of license.  In case renewal is done away with, the details of these person’s integral 
to food safety would not be captured.  Moreover, at the time of renewal, the licensing 
authority can verify the food safety history of the food business based on which he can renew 

10 
 
the license or decide otherwise.  In the absence of a renewal mechanism, enforcement would 
have to be implemented by means of suspension and cancellation of license. Renewal of 
license/registration acts as a monitoring mechanism.  As a compliance of the FSS Act, Rule s 
and Regulations made thereunder, an FBO has to provide certain details like water testing 
reports, medical examination reports of food handlers and filing of annual returns etc. at the 
time of renewal.  The apprehension is that once licenses are made per manent, the FBO would 
not have much motivation to file these returns as FBO would stand disconnected from 
FSSAI/Regulator after the issue of permanent license. Enforcement again would then perforce 
be done through suspension and cancellation of license. Th erefore, there is no proposal to 
issue life time licenses.

1.86 The Committee is not convinced with the sampling procedure, analysis time and 
protocols followed in the national milk quality surveys conducted by FSSAI in 2011 and 
2016 as they were not uniform. The Committee observes that a precise and accurate 
conclusion out of survey(s) can be drawn only with appropriate sample size. Sample size of 
1791 and 1663 in the surveys of 2011 and 2016 were not adequate. Taking into account the 
size of population and the quantity of milk produced in the country, the Committee would, 
therefore, exhort the Ministry to ensure that in future the sample size of such sur veys should 
be appropriate and truly representative. The Ministry has to ensure that protocols followed for 
such surveys are uniform so that they lead to valid conclusions. The Committee also desires 
to be kept apprised of the findings of the national milk quality survey initiated in May, 2018. 
(Para 5.12) 
Action Taken 
1.87 FSSAI has conducted a survey on quality of milk. It initiated a Nationwide 
Qualitative Screening of milk samples for on -spot qualitative and quantitative analysis of 
milk. The survey was  initiated in May, 2018 with a sample size   of   6432 samples taken 
from 1100 towns with a population of over 50,000 across all 29 States and 7 Union 
Territories for qualitative and quantitative analysis. Scope of NMSQS 2018 covered 3 quality 
parameters ( Fat, SNF and water), 13 common adulterants (vegetable oil/fat, 
detergents/caustic soda, hydrogen peroxide, sugar, glucose, urea, starch, Maltodextrin, boric 
acid, ammonium sulphate, nitrates, cellulose, and neutralizer; and 3 contaminants (antibiotics, 
pesticides, aflatoxin M1,).  All the 6432 samples were collected and analysed qualitatively 
immediately onsite in mobile vans and nearly 30% of those samples that tested positive for 
any of the adulterants and/or contaminants were tested quantitatively in lab oratory to 
ascertain whether the samples were compliant or non-compliant to limits set.    
1.88 As per NMSQS final report released in October, 2019 -   
- About 7%  samples were found to be unsafe for consumption due to presence of 
harmful contaminants in e xcess of specified limits coming mainly from poor quality 
of feed, irresponsible use of antibiotics and poor farm practices 
- Only 12 out of total 6432 samples had adulterants that affect the quality of milk 
- About 41% of milk samples of the total were, h owever, non -compliant with 
reference to one or the other quality parameters [fat, Solid not -fat (SNF), sugar and 
maltodextrin] but were without any safety issues.   
1.89 Details of survey are  available at https://www.fssai.gov.in/home .   Thus, the survey  
results indicate clearly that milk being sold in India is largely safe for consumption.  This is 
contrary to the popular perception carried by the consumers owing to misrepresented 
information for various reasons including deceitful campaigns and unsubstantiated reports 
Recommendation/Observation

1.104 Under sub-regulation 2.3.5 of Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restriction 
on Sales) Regulations, 20 11, use of acetylene gas, commonly known as carbide gas, in 
artificial ripening of fruits has been prohibited.  As an alternative, ripening of fruits by using 
ethylene gas at a concentration upto 100 ppm (100µ/L) depending upon the crop, variety and 
maturity is now permitted.  Ethylene is a safer alternative. it may be mentioned that ethylene 
is a hormone which is produced in the fruits naturally to facilitate their ripening   in a natural 
way.   
1.105 As also suggested by the Standing Committee, periodic advisories have been issued to 
the State Food Authorities to monitor use of calcium carbide   for artificial ripening of fruits 
and take stringent action for violation of the provisions. Further, whenev er a specific instance 
is reported about use of banned carbide gas for ripening, the matter is immediately taken up 
with Food Safety Commissioners of States/UTs for taking strict action in respect of reported 
instances.  
1.106 Further, a Guidance Note on a rtificial ripening of fruits has been published to create 
awareness among food business operators/ traders, consumers and other stakeholders related 
to various aspects of artificial ripening of fruits. It also includes Standard Operating 
Procedure detailing all facets of artificial ripening using ethylene gas and its reliable sources. 
In addition, a direction was issued on 16.08.2018 on use of ‘ethephon’ in powder form for 
artificial ripening of fruits and the same was uploaded on FSSAI’s website for wider 
publicity. It clarifies that ethephon in powder form may also be used as a source of ethylene 
gas provided that it shall be packed in sachets and shall not come in direct contact with fruits.  
1.107 It may be stated that Calcium Carbide/Formaldehyde etc. h ave many industrial uses. 
Regulating/restricting the manufacture and sale of such products does not come within the 
purview of FSSAI.

1.109 With a view to check misuse of non-edible ice as edible ice, a decision has been 
taken and conveyed   to all States/UTs that food colour (Indigo Carmine or Brilliant blue up

food commodities, to give it a bluish look/appearance so as to enable clear differentiation 
with edible ice which must remain colourless. All Food Business Operators engaged in

w.e.f. 1st June, 2018. Food Safety Commissioners of States/UTs have been asked to  enhance

1.111 To streamline the food import system, FSSAI has an online system known as F ood 
Import Clearance System (FICS). The FICS is integrated with the customs’ ICE -GATE 
(Indian Customs Electronic Commerce/Electronic Data interchange (EC/EDI) Gateway) 
system. 
 
1.112 Risk Management System (RMS) is implemented in ICE -GATE wherein, based on 
the risk categorization of the food, compliance history of the importer and country of origin 
etc. co nsignments are referred to FSSAI for clearance. Such food articles  are subjected to 
scrutiny of documents, visual inspection, sampling and testing in order to determine their 
conformance to the safety and quality standards laid down under various Food Safe ty and 
Standards Regulations. If sample is found conforming a No Objection Certificate (NOC) is 
generated and in case of otherwise, Non -Conforming Report (NCR) is generated.  For food 
consignments imported into India, a special condition has been introduce d through an 
amendment in Regulation 2 (b) (6) of Food Safety and Standards (Import) Regulations, 2017 
whereby food products having a valid shelf life of not less than sixty per cent or three months 
before expiry at the time of import, whichever is less, s hall not be cleared by Customs. As a 
result, entry of food products nearing expiry or after expiry date is prohibited. Food Import 
samples are tested with reference to the Standards prescribed under various FSS Regulations. 
The Standards notified by FSSAI are globally benchmarked while being consistent with 
Indian context. It is unlikely that a food product which is banned outside is allowed to enter 

22 
 
into the country as the Indian Standards are harmonized with Codex and other International 
Standards.

1.116 Information in respect of recall plan has been furnished in reply to Para 3.23 above.

Action Taken 
1.118 FSSAI has taken many steps for reducing the clearance time of Imported Food items 
such as: 
a) Introduction of provisional No Objection Certificate (PNOC) for imported pre -
packaged retail food articles vide directions dated 01.05.2018, in addition to Provisional 
No Objection Certificates (PNOC) for imported food items having short shelf -life (less 
than 7 days) such as fresh fruits & vegetables which require special storage conditions.  
With the PNOC, an importer can move t he imported food consignment to a   well -
equipped storage facility till receipt of the lab test results, but can’t release the same in 
the market. This step results into reduction of the demurrage charges. 
 

23

   c)   A regular monitoring of time taken for testing of imported food items by labs is being

1.119 As a result of the above measures, time taken in import clearance has been reduced

Recommendation/Observation 
2.1 The Committee notes that FSSAI is the apex regulatory body for food safety in the 
country and the Preamble to FSS Act inter -alia seeks to lay down science based standards for 
articles of food and ensure availability of safe and wholesome food for human con sumption.  
Food Safety is thus a specialized job and FSSAI being a science based organization should be 
equipped with proper tools and capabilities and headed by someone with the requisite 
technical acumen and appropriate expertise to address the challengi ng task of food regulation 
for a country like India.  Engaging man-power with technical skill and competence, therefore, 
becomes imperative for effective rendering of important mandate given to FSSAI.  The 
Committee is of the opinion that the regulatory body should be run by experts/scientists in the 
food sector with bureaucratic support.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
qualifications   and procedures of selection and appointment of Chairman and CEO of FSSAI 
be reviewed so that the best profe ssional with domain expertise are selected for this onerous 
regulatory responsibility. While reviewing and modifying the process of selection and 
appointment of Chairman and CEO, the Government may take a cue from similar regulatory 
mechanisms functioning in some of the developed countries like USA, UK, Australia etc.  
 
(Para 1.22)

has been laid down in section 5 & 6 of the Food Safety and Standards Ac t, 2006. In terms of

the persons of eminence in the field of food science or from amongst the persons from 
administration who have been/are associated with the subjec t in the level not below the rank 
of Secretary to the Government of India. Chairperson and CEO are appointed on the basis of 
administrative experience in diverse fields . They work with aid and advice of technical 
experts available in Scientific Panels of F SSAI on different subjects. Experience, so far, has 
shown that they have functioned very effectively in discharge of their responsibilities.  
 
Recommendation /Observation

have some members with industrial experience so that the diverse views from other se ctors 
are also accommodated.

2.14 The implementation and enforcement of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 rests 
primarily with the State/UT Governments, for which regular surveillance, monitoring and  
inspection are required to be undertaken by them.  The Committee however notes that many 
States do not have a separate food safety Department.  The Committee is of the view that 
food adulteration, lack of quality checks, misleading labelling, sale of defective food products 
etc. that have become the norm these days are primarily an offshoot of absence of a dedicated 
and robust food safety apparatus at the State Level. The Joint Committee of Parliament on the 
Prevention of Food Adulteration (Amendment), 197 4 had recommended long back that for 
effective implementation of the Act, a separate food safety department under the control of 
the Director of Health should be established in all the States.  Endorsing the same view, the 
Committee strongly recommends est ablishment of a separate agency or Department of Food 
Safety in each State for enforcing a robust food safety mechanism in the country.  The 
Committee also recommends that the creation of a dedicated food regulatory mechanism in 
each State be taken up by t he Union Government with the State Governments at the highest 
level.    
 

28 
 
2.15 The Committee notes that there is no uniformity in the food safety infrastructure 
across the country.  Some States do not even have a food safety department and a food safety 
appellate tribunal.  The food testing laboratories lack functional equipments as well as 
technical manpower.  This inadequate arrangement has failed to control food adulteration in 
the country.   Therefore, the Committee recommends removal of this existing in consistency 
and introduction of a uniform structure across the country.  The Central Government should 
work in cooperation with the State Government to establish a uniform food safety regulatory 
regime in the country.  It is also very important for the foo d testing laboratories across 
States/UTs to follow uniform procedure/methodology and guidelines so that consistent results 
are obtained.   
(Para 2.17 & 2.20) 
Action Taken

States/UTs regularly. As per the data shared by States/UTs in Quarterly Progress 
Report on State Specific recommendations of CAG and the PSC, process of creation 
of separate food safety department has been initiated in 6 States/UTsviz Andhra 
Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Goa &Uttrakhand.

2.78 There is no overlap in FSSAI and BIS or AGMARK standards because the mandate 
of FSSAI standards is different than of BIS or AGMARK standards. FSSAI standards are 
mandatory standards and are minimum standards, There is no provision of grades. While 
AGMARK a nd BIS standards  are voluntary and have grades  based on their superiority in 
quality. However, the BIS and AGMARK standards are considered by the relevant Scientific 
Panels while framing the standards of food products to be notified in Regulations under FS S 
Act,2006. 
Recommendation /Observation 
2.79 The Committee understands that assessing the safety of food contact material is very 
crucial as there is always a high   possibility of chemicals leaking from the material down to 
the food. This can change the c omposition of the food and make the food unsuitable for 
consumption. Moreover, the food packaging material on reaction with food article can 
introduce toxicity. Therefore, the Committee recommends that FSSAI should specify the 
toxicity levels of the food c ontact materials under different conditions especially during 
storage, processing and transportation where the food package can be exposed to different 
environmental conditions. The Committee also recommends constitution of a scientific 
working group to study the impact of food packaging on health aspects. FSSAI needs to bring 
standards and specifications for food packaging materials so that any unwanted toxic 
contamination by use of substandard packaging material is avoided.   
(Para 6.10) 
Action Taken 
2.80 Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations that specify that all packaging 
materials of plastic origin shall pass the prescribed overall migration limit of 60mg/kg or 
10mg/dm2when tested as per Indian standard, IS 9845, with no visible colour migra tion has 
been finalised. This also includes that newspaper or any such material shall not be used for 
storing and wrapping of food. 
2.81 These regulations are aimed at establishing requirements for packaging materials 
ensuring that they are safe for use in  packaging and do not cause any health hazard to 
consumer or lead to change in sensory property or composition of foods. T he list of safe 
packaging materials has also been broadened.  A suggestive list of packaging materials for 
different food categories is also specified therein. 
2.82 It may be pertinent to mention here that, FSSAI has conducted a study jointly with 
Indian Institute of Packaging (IIP) and National Test House (NTH) to determine the 
migration of chemical contaminants and heavy metals from pa ckaging into food.  Based on 
the results followed by key recommendations of the Packaging Review Group, definitions 
of food grade, overall migration limit,  primary food packaging, specific migration limit  have 
been included in the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulation, 2018  along with 
other inclusions.   
Recommendation /Observation 
2.83  The Committee recommends that any changes in the Packaging and Labelling 
regulations should be timely disclosed to the FBOs so that they get enough time to conform 
to the changed standards. The regulations should be implemented in a phased manner rather 

40 
 
than haphazardly. Proper training to the FBOs is essential for enforcement of the labelling 
norms.  
(Para 6.13) 
Action Taken

2.85 The Committee understands that the illiterate section of the country may find it

labelling based on colours and symbols. The Committee also recommends the traffic light 
labelling system as practised in other countries for packaged food items in India. This

unhealthy, food amber for moderate, and green for low (healthy).

 2.87 However, on the basis of comments received from various stakeholders including

domestically produced, it should follow a uniform standard and should be tested on the same

benchmarked.  Internationally available standards including Codex Standards, USFDA, EU

inspectors and unethical Food Business Operators. Once a food product is found to have 
violated food safety procedures by the Food Regulator, there is no effective recourse 
available because the appeal procedure is entirely internal and departmental and even a legal

3.124  The Committee observes that loose edible oils are prone to adulteration and even if

resulted in masses being afflicted by dropsy. The Committee gathers that Delhi –based  
consumer organisation, namely, Consumer Voice, had in the year 201 6 collected samples of 
loose edible oils of eight varieties, namely Mustard, Sesame, Groundnut and Cottonseed from

difficult to trace the source of the problem. in the event of health epidemic breaking out due 
to adulterated edible oils.

recommend to the Central Govt to impress upon the State Governments to ensure that edible

3.135  The Committee observes that in India the GM food imports require approvals under 
the Environment Protection Act of 1986 and the Food Safety and Standards Act of 2006. 
While the former law covers the environmental impacts of the food products, the latter 
assesses the food’s impact on human health. Since no regulation has been finalized for GM 
products, it is still banned in the country. Further, even after the Environment Ministry gives 
clearances for imports, permission is also required under the food safe ty law but importers 
have got away without having the mandatory approval under the Food Safety and Standards 
Act. A large number of products are coming in India with GM ingredients but neither 
consumers nor authorities are aware of what is inside because t here is nothing mentioned on 
the label. Taking the above fact into account, the Committee recommends formulation of 
regulations to the effect that those importing foods must provide mandatory declaration on 
the label mentioning that ‘this food is from GM f ree source’. Countries like China, Australia 
and the European Union nations have strict regulations about GM foods labelling so that the 
consumer makes informed choices.   
3.136 The Committee observes that even after more than a decade of enactment of FSS Act, 
a regulatory vacuum exists in the import of GM Food. FSSAI has neither put the regulations 
for such approvals in place nor taken any measures to stop the imports. The Committee 
recommends that the FSSAI should urgently finalise “Guidelines for safety assessment of 
food derived by GM technology” and implement them within three months of presentation of 
the Report to the Parliament. FSSAI should also work to upgrade the GM food testing 
infrastructure and make use of the already present laboratories in th e country and equip them 
with latest technology.   
3.137 The Committee is perturbed to note that the action (or lack of it) in regulation of GM 
foods by FSSAI has been painstakingly slow. Recently FSSAI had decided to have the 
labelling norms for genetically modified food products in order to give informed choice to the

irreversible damage to the consumers, who are the core constituency for whom FSSAI was 
set up. The Committee strongly censures the FSSAI for this lackadaisical attitude and 
implores upon it to pull up its socks and ensure that the regulation made in respect to GM

this regulation of certifying organic food as this will remov e non -certified /fake products 
from the market. Further, the Committee also recommends that a separate certification 
mechanism should be in place for small farmers who cannot afford these two certification 
options at an additional cost.   
(Para 5.67) 
Action Taken 
 
3.145 PGS is targeted at farmers including small farmers and FSSAI is working with the 
Ministry of Agriculture to make Participatory Guarantee System (PGS) more small -farmer 
friendly.  At the same time, FSSAI is considering allowing Participatory Guarantee Systems 
Organic Council (PGSOC), which represents tens of thousands of small and marginal farmers 
in the country, as a third system for certification of organic food. 
 
3.146 To ensure consumer’s trust, there is need of genuineness and authenticity of foods 
claimed as ‘Organic’. To ensure this, a regulatory mechanism backed by a robust certification 
system is required. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has the mandate to 
regulate manufacture, distribute, sale or import  “organic foods” as per the provisions laid 
under Section 22 of the Food Safety Standards Act, 2006. Organic foods are regulated by 
Food Safety and Standards (Organic Foods) Regulations, 2017 notified under the provisions 
of the Act. Food Safety and Standards (Organic Foods) Regulations, 2017 stipulate  that - 
 the organic food offered or promoted for sale shall comply with the provisions of one 
of the systems namely Participatory Guarantee System for India (PGS -India) 
implemented by Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare or the National 
Programme for Organic Production (NPOP) implemented by APEDA under Ministry 
of Commerce and Industry.    As per the Regulations, a product may carry a 
certification or quality assurance mark of one of the systems mention ed above in 
addition to the Food Safety and Standard Authority of India’s organic logo (Jaivik 
Bharat logo).  The consumers can easily identify the organic foods by looking at the 
Jaivik Bharat logo and can get assured about these being genuinely organic. 
 To address the difficulties of the small and marginal farmers/ small FBOs, Organic 
food which is marketed through direct sales to the end consumer by the small original 
producer or producer organisation is exempted from provision of the certification 
system i.e., NPOP or PGS -India. Small original producer or producer organisation is 
the one whose annual turnover is not exceeding Rs 12 Lakhs per annum. 

72 
 
(The Food Safety and Standards (Organic Foods) Regulations, 2017 can be obtained from 
Website: www.fssai.gov.in.) 
 
3.147 The initiatives taken recently  to address the difficulties of small producers/FBOs are : 
I. The proposal for inclusion of a provision for ‘aggregator/intermediary’ and ‘In -
conversion’ products in the Food S afety and Standards (Organic Foods) Regulations, 
2017 was approved by Food Authority and is under Draft Notification Stage. The 
objective for the said amendment are stated below: 
 An amendment to permit Aggregator/Intermediary to collect organic food from s mall 
farmers and sell it to the end consumer directly has been proposed as small farmers 
have low quantities of organic produce to sell and cannot afford to go to the market. 
Such aggregator shall be such whose annual turnover is less than Rs 50 Lakhs per 
annum and shall maintain records of traceability and other documents and abide by 
the Standards. They cannot use Jaivik Bharat Logo. 
3.148 Another amendment is to mention “In conversion to Organic” on the labels for the 
products which are in conversion und er NPOP or PGS -India. Since Jaivik Bharat Logo 
cannot be used on such labels, mentioning “In -conversion to organic” on the labels will 
provide Food Business Operators with some extra edge over conventional foods and will get 
better price. It may be mention ed that ‘conversion’ is the process of changing an agricultural 
farm from conventional to organic   and varies from one year to three years depending on the 
type of crop. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.149 The Committee appreciates that FSSAI understands the difficulties faced by 
small FBOs in accessing the market. The Committee, however, is quite apprehensive of 
the proposal for inclusion of a provision for "aggregator/ intermediary" in the FSS 
(Organic Foods) Regulations, 2017.  The Committee, in this regard , recommends that 
FSSAI should take necessary measures to ensure that the small FBOs are not exploited 
and get adequate remuneration of their produce. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.150 The Committee notes that safety net programs –both Mid -day Meal(MDM) and 
Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS) have mandated the use of fortified wheat 
flour, oil and doubled fortified salt nationally, ensuring that the most vulnerable sections of

safety net programs involve economies of scale and are not in the domain of Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare. However, in the present scheme of things, provisio n of even 
basic items under these two programs is prone to massive pilferage/sub -
standardisation/leakages. Various media reports have highlighted many cases of food 
poisoning involving contamination and adulteration of meals under the MDM Scheme 
making several children severely ill. Even under ICDS, health of small children and lactating 
others is at stake due to unsafe food items. How FSSAI would ensure provision of fortified 
foods under these programs remains to be seen as conversion of intent into actual  realisation 
is what counts the most. The Committee while not discounting the importance of these 
schemes would like the FSSAI to embark upon a time -bound due diligence process on the 
States which have an efficient distribution of resources under these two  safety net programs 

73 
 
and introduce the fortified items in these States and replicate the success of these programs in 
other States in a time bound manner. 
(Para 5.71)

scale up plan for fortification.

 Action Taken  
3.172 FSSAI has taken several initiatives to digitize data. Physical submission of 
documents for License has been done away with and all the documents are now required to 
be submitted online on FLRS. The inspection procedure is also being digitized through Food 
Safety Compliance Through Regular Inspection and Sampling (FoSCoRIS) and data on 
inspection reports will be available online. In addition, the data of sampling and testing is 
also being digitized through Indian Food Laboratory Network (InFoLNet) portal.  
3.173 The online Food Licensing and Registration System (FLRS) is  fully functional across 
the country. Further, FSSAI is launching Food Safety and Compliance System (FoSCoS) 
which will replace existing online Food Licensing and Registration System (FLRS) in a 
phased manner in different States/UTs. FoSCoS functions on cl oud based server with 
upgraded software and hardware and will resolve the often reported issue of slowness of 
existing FLRS portal. FoSCoS is envisaged to be the one -stop ‘Compliance Portal’ for food 
safety and in future will be escalated to have more modu les for functional needs such as 
advanced MIS, audit module, linkage with InFolNet, hygiene rating etc. FoSCoS essentially 
has the same flows as FLRS, so that users have convenience in using FoSCoS. The cardinal 
change is the methodology of licensing for m anufacturers which now shall be based on 
standardised product list. Module for filing of Annual Return is incorporated in FoSCoS. 
Mandatory documents have been rationalised and many paper based declarations have been 
replaced with online declaration. The c entral theme is to enhance the ease of doing business 
for the food business operators without compromising food safety. 
  
Further Recommendation

4.1 The Committee notes that the use of food dyes has to be regulated because time and

(Para 2.26) 
Action Taken 
 
4.2 To review existing Food Safety and Standards Regulations on Foo d Colours, a 
Working Group (WG) was constituted by the Scientific Committee under the Scientific Panel 
on Food Additives, Flavourings, Processing Aids and Materials in Contact with Food dated 
05.07.2018 with the following Terms of Reference: 
(i) To collect and collate relevant scientific data, either from the industry or available in 
the public domain, for risk assessment of food colors. 
(ii) The evaluation of the data and risk assessment of the food colors for their use in 
various food categories. 
(iii) To recommend appropriate nomenclature for the natural and synthetic food colours. 
(iv) To review the current levels of usage for food colours and propose new limits, if 
required. 
(v) To review the existing vertical standards of food colours and to develop vertical 
standards for all remaining colours. 
 
2. Till date 4 meetings of Working Group has been convened. The work done so far is as 
under: 
(i) Task related to nomenclature for the natural and synthetic food colours has been 
completed by WG. The same has also been deliberated and approved by the Scientific 
Panel.  
 
(ii) Review of the existing standards of food colours and to develop vertical standards for 
all remaining colours is under consideration and following parts has been completed 
deliberated and approved by the Scientific Panel: 
 
 The standard for colour preparations was reviewed and revised accordingly to 
include both natural and synthetic food colours. 
 Provision for lake colours was revised based on specification laid down by 
Joint FAO/WHO Expert committee on Food Additives (JECFA).  

79 
 
 It was suggested that for using combination of colours, the maximum limit for 
use in a particular food category m ay not be fixed because of the absence of 
any scientific basis and rationale. 
 
(iii) Collection and collation of data for risk assessment of food colours has been done. 
However, its review and evaluation will be taken up by the WG basis on which 
existing levels of usage for food colours in different food categories will be reviewed. 
 
3.  After completion of the task by the WG, the final report will be placed before the 
Scientific Panel. After approval by the Scientific Panel, it will be placed before Scientific 
Committee for further evaluation and subsequently Food Authority for approval. 
4. The aforesaid task is of scientific nature which requires collection and collation of 
relevant data and their detailed examination in view of various aspects of human risks. It is 
therefore, difficult to assign a fixed time frame for completion of the work.  Five meetings of 
the WG have been conducted so far. WG carried out a detailed review of the standards and 
provisions related to food colours.   The WG has almost completed i ts task. The 
recommendations of the WG are as under: 
 
(i) Nomenclature: WG suggested to have no distinction between natural and synthetic 
food colours and decided to call them simply as “food colours”. It was recommended 
that each food colour shall be declared on the label of the product using their INS 
number with full nomenclature as prescribed under regulations. 
(ii) Colouring foods will not fall under the definition of food colours.  
(iii) Maximum limit of food colours in combination : It was decided that no maximum 
limit for colours in combination can be fixed in absence of any scientific basis. 
(iv) Food Colour - Preparation and Mixtures: It was suggested revising the standard to 
generalise for food colours irrespective of its type-natural or synthetic. 
(v) Aluminium Lakes of Colouring Matters :  Provision for lake colours was revised 
based on specification laid down by Joint FAO/WHO Expert committee on Food 
Additives (JECFA).  
(vi) Vertical standards on Food Colours : The specifications for all the fo od colours 
listed in Food Safety and Standards Regulations (FSSR) including those which do not 
have any standards at present were thoroughly examined. After detailed deliberations, 
it was decided to adopt the JECFA specifications for all the food colours. Each 
parameter was thoroughly examined for the food colours for its adoption in FSSR. 
(vii) Risk assessment of food colours permitted in FSSR 
WG carried out risk assessment of the food colours having lowest Acceptable Daily 
Intakes (ADI), i.e. Canthaxanthi n and Erythrosine. Accordingly, their limits in 
different food categories were reviewed and revised.
