presentation of the Report to the Parliament but the Ministry is yet to notify a few 
regulations. The Committee expresses its deep anguish over the lackadaisical approach 
of FSSAI and recommends to notify the remaining notification at the earliest.  
 
(Para 3.3) 
LICENSING AND REGISTRATION ISSUES 
 
 The Committee notes that the Ministry has neither spelt out the details of SOP 
for prescribing timeline at each stage nor has given rea sons for delay in notification of 
rules.  The Committee is of the view that timely notification of rules and regulation 
would pave the way for better implementation of the Act and further strengthen the 
food safety ecosystem in the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends FSSAI to 
strictly adhere to the recommendations of the Lok Sabha Committee on Subordinate 
Legislation. 
  
(Para 3.6) 
 
 The Committee notes that the Appellate Tribunal has been constituted in 30 
States/UTs. The Committee expects the Min istry to expedite the process of establishing 
the Appellate tribunal in the remaining States so that the litigation process can be fast 
tracked. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to facilitate the formation of 
District Level Advisory Committees in the remaining States/UTs.  
 
(Para 3.12) 
 
 The Committee understands that adoption of GAP, GAHP, GAFP, etc, is 
primarily vested with Department of Agriculture, Department of Animal Husbandry 
and Dairying which functions in collaboration with States/UTs. But since these good 
practices would ultimately go a long way in helping FSSAI achieve its objectives, it is 
imperative that FSSAI makes all out efforts to see that these practices are adopted and 
implemented. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the work of developing 
Guidance document on Good Agricultural Practices is completed at the earliest so that 
the training and awareness programme could be started. 
 
(Para 3.16) 
 
 The Committee takes note of the various measures taken by FSSAI to prevent 
unethical practices and hopes that they will be able to contain corrupt practices to some 
extent.  But since cases of adulteration in food items are on the rise, the Committee feels 
that there is a need to force some stringent measures in this regard.  The  Committee, 
therefore, reiterates its recommendations and urges upon FSSAI to nudge the 
States/UTs to take corruption in food safety matters seriously. 
 (Para 3.21) 
 

84 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over non formulation of the SOP even after 
two years of the presentation of the Report and therefore, recommends to expedite the 
process to enable the enforcement authorities to act uniformly in the matter.  
 
(Para 3.24) 
 
 The Committee has been given to understand that out of the 36 States/UTs, 25 
States have so far adopted digital inspection system of FOSCORs. The Committee finds 
that one of the major challenges of putting in place the FOSCORIS system has been the 
non-availability of mobile network in the remote areas and also of other amenities.  The 
Committee appreciates that apart from an online module, an offline one has also been 
developed to address the problem. The Committee, however, feels that in order to 
successfully implement the application, it is essential that States/UTs concentrate on 
providing basic amenities to its FSO. The Committee desires that States/UTs can sign 
an MoU with a mobile network company to have uninterrupted connectivity in remote 
areas so that the FSOs can carry out their duties efficiently.  
(Para 3.31) 
 
 
 The Committee desires that the proposed amendments to Section 42(3) of FSS 
Act be expedited so that perishable food items with a short span of life are tested before 
getting spoiled.  
(Para 3.34) 
FOOD SAFETY SURVEY 
 
 On perusal of the State wise details of Adjudicating Officers, Designated 
Officers, Food Safety Officers, etc The Committee noted the following:- 
(i) 15 States have full time Food Safety Commissioners while 21 States have 
given additional charge of Food Safety to other officials. 
 (ii) Total of 705 Adjudicating Officers in the States 
(iii) Total 432 full time DOs in all States. States like Bihar, Chhattisgarh, 
Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, Odisha, Rajasthan and Tripura 
have nil full time DOs.  Part time DOs 138 in all States, like Chhattisgarh, 
Haryana, Karnataka, Odisha, Rajasthan. Therefore, States like Bihar, 
Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, Tripura do not have a single DO (either full 
time or part time). 
(iv) Total 2563 full time FSOs in all the States with the exception of Rajasthan 
Part time FSOs 100 in States like Karnataka, Rajasthan and Sikkim. 
(v) As regards Appellate Tribunal, all States except Himachal Pradesh, 
Jharkhand, Lakshadweep, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Ladakh h ave 
an Appellate Tribunal. 
(Para 3.37) 
 
 It is evident from the above that there are lot of variations amongst the States 
with respect to the number of AOs, DOs, FSOs, etc. The Committee is concerned to note 
that whereas the States like Bihar, Madhya Prade sh, Mizoram and Tripura do not have 
a single DO.  To the utmost surprise, the State of Rajasthan does not have a single full 

85 
 
time FSO.  The Committee also notes that Karnataka is the only State which has full 
time as well as part time DOs and FSOs.  The Co mmittee, therefore, would like FSSAI 
to pro-actively persuade States like Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, Tripura to have 
Designated Officers appointed in their States and also persuade Rajasthan to appoint 
full time FSOs in its State. Further, States, not  having an Appellate Tribunal, may also 
be persuaded to have one in their States. 
(Para 3.38) 
 
  The Committee takes note of the civil and criminal cases and action taken 
thereon. As per the information given, total number of cases registered in 2018 -19 was 
21,363 (2813 - Criminal Cases + 18550- Civil Cases) and out of that, there were only 701 
convictions and 12,734 penalties imposed.  The status of remaining 7928 cases has not 
been shared with the Ministry.  The Committee, however, believes that there is no strict 
adherence to the FSS regulations and cases are not being dealt within 90 days. The 
Committee emphasized upon the need, therefore, reiterates its recommendation 
including the one for having a full time Adjudicating Officer to enable them to do 
justice to their assigned duties.  
(Para 3.39) 
 
INSPECTIONS 
 The Committee takes into cognizance the efforts being made like regular 
surveillance, monitoring, inspection of food premises, sampling of food products, 
regular training of officers concerned, upgradation of food labs etc.  The Committee is 
of the firm view that in addition to these interventions, pro -active and concerted efforts 
need to be made by FSSAI to regularly prompt the States/UTs for gearing their 
machinery to develop a system which has  zero tolerance towards violation of any food 
safety norms by FBOs. Timely and appropriate punishment would definitely prove to 
be a deterrent for the violators of food safety laws and this could be achieved only by 
increasing the conviction rate. The Comm ittee, therefore, reiterates that FSSAI should 
take up the issue of low conviction rate with the Ministry of Law & Justice to find a 
solution to the problem as early as possible.  Further, the Committee would also like the 
FSSAI to assess the surveillance Reports submitted by States/UTs to FSSAI and identify 
the best performing State/UTs so that the benchmarking model could be followed by 
other low performing States.    
(Para 3.45) 
 
 Considering the extent of food adulteration prevalent now -a-days in the 
country, the number of cancelled licenses with State and Central is very low and thus 
genuinely raises apprehension over food safety monitoring mechanism.  
(Para 3.48) 
 
LIFTING OF SAMPLES 
 
 The Committee notes that Section 16 (2) (g) of FSS Act provides for conducting 
survey of enforcement and administration of this Act in the country. The Committee 
observes that FSSAI has not yet framed the regulations under the section rather it has 
suggested for deletion of the section in the amendments proposed under FSS Act. The 
Committee reiterates its recommendation and strongly believes that surveys will 
provide a better understanding of the food safety management system in the country., 

86 
 
The Committee,  therefore, strongly recommends FSSAI to make regulations under 
Section 16 (2)(g) for conducting surveys by the Central/State agencies as well as 
outsourcing the work to a third party. 
(Para 3.58) 
 
  The Committee appreciates FSSAI’s initiative of creating  a State Food Safety 
Index and recommends FSSAI to rank States and UTs as per this index and identify the 
States and UTs on ranking credit basis i.e best performance States and poor 
performance States. The Committee also recommends FSSAI to make use of thi s index 
in launching State specific initiatives and programs that will help the State in identifying 
the loopholes and strengthening its weak areas. 
(Para 3.59) 
 
TRAINING OF FBOS 
 
 The Committee is of the considered view that FSSAI should take up the issue  of 
shortage of manpower in the States/UTs on a priority basis.  The Committee would also 
like to suggest that ranking of States/UTs on the basis of infrastructure, manpower and 
performance be periodically prepared by FSSAI and also displayed on its websit e to 
motivate the best performing States and also encourage the poor performing 
States/lagging on these parameters, especially manpower. 
 
(Para 3.64) 
 
SHORTAGE OF MANPOWER 
 
 The Committee notes that 25 States/UTs have adopted digital inspection system 
of FoSCoRIS.  The Committee, however, desires that FSSAI must try to ensure that 
digital inspection system of FoSCoRIS in the remaining States/UTs is implemented at 
the earliest.   
(Para 3.67) 
 
 The Committee takes note of the efforts made by FSSAI on strengthening the 
human resource in the State Food Regulatory Bodies.  The efforts are showing some 
positive results also.  The Committee, therefore, desires that FSSAI must continue to 
pursue and convince States/UTs to strengthen their manpower. 
(Para 3.70) 
 
 The Committee hopes that recruitment of additional 493 posts at various levels 
would address the shortage of manpower to a great extent. The Committee, however, 
would like the Ministry to chalk out long term action plan in tandem with State/UTs 
Government to overcome the shortage of manpower in State Food Regulatory Bodies. 
However, short term plan the FSSAI should ensure that States/UTs engage 
professionally qualified persons on short-term contract till adequate manpower is made 
available.   
 
(Para 3.74) 
 
 The Committee is of the view that appointing SDOs as part time DOs should not 
be viewed as a permanent solution to shortage of manpower. SDO has multiple 
responsibilities and duties to perform and additional charge as DO would not do justice 
to the u rgency required for an efficient food safety monitoring mechanism. The 

87 
 
Committee is not in agreement with the idea of doing away with technical qualification 
for a DO and recommends Ministry to consider restoration of the minimum 
qualification of bachelors  degree in Science with Chemistry as one subject for 
appointment as DO, in the first instance and if the candidates are not available, at least, 
the candidates must have science stream at the higher secondary level. 
(Para 3.77) 
 
EFFICACY OF FOOD TESTING LABS 
 
  The Committee has been informed about the proposal to establish two National 
Food laboratories (NFLs) at Chennai and Mumbai. The Committee has however been 
not updated on the upgradation of NFL at Ghaziabad and Kolkata. The Committee lays 
great emphasis on establishing a robust Food testing infrastructure in the country and 
therefore, strongly recommends FSSAI to expedite the implementation of the proposals. 
It would like the Ministry to submit a note on current status of all four laboratories.   
(Para 3.81) 
TESTING PROTOCOLS AND PROCEDURES 
 
 The Committee is of the view that only publication of Manuals will not facilitate 
a uniform Laboratory Testing System in the country. FSSAI will have to ensure that 
these manuals on Method of Analysis and Good Laboratory Practices are diligently 
followed by all the FTLs in the country. The Committee observes that FSSAI has not 
paid the desired attention to the prevailing inadequate facilities for checking the food 
articles on all parameters in the labs. The pers isting flawed practice of deeming a food 
article safe even when it fails on some parameters raises serious concern about the 
accuracy of the testing methodology. The Committee, therefore, recommends FSSAI to 
guide the Laboratories about the specific food s afety parameters on which any food 
article should be mandatorily checked. Imported food should only be allowed in the 
market when it has passed the mandatory parameters as per the global norms. 
 
(Para 3.85) 
 
 The Committee recommends that FSSAI should expe dite the process of 
amending the FSS Rule, 2011 for incorporating the provision of 14 days time period for 
a referral laboratory to submit their test reports.  The Committee further reiterates its 
recommendation for adoption of best international practices  by the National Referral 
Laboratories with respect to standards for testing and validation.  
(Para 3.89) 
 
NABL ACCREDITATION OF LABS 
 
 The Committee strongly recommends FSSAI to accelerate the drive to accredit 
the remaining FTLs that have not been notified by it so far. The Committee also urges 
the Ministry and FSSAI to take up the matter of accreditation with the States and 
ensure speedy notification of the State Food Testing Laboratories under Section 43(1) of 
FSS Act, 2006. Operation of most of the existing labs without NABL accreditation raises 
serious apprehension over the FTLs quality and technical competence. The Committee 
is worried that most of these labs may not have undergone a third party 
assessment/audit. The Committee also opines that F SSAI should take strict measures 
against the labs that have repeatedly been failing in quality assessment/audit. Labs that 
are already NABL accredited should also be investigated periodically. 

88 
 
 
(Para 3.92) 
STATUS OF MANPOWER IN LABS 
 As per data submitted by FSSAI, there are 452 Public/Food Analysts against the 
estimated requirement of almost 800 food analyst. The Committee concludes that many 
laboratories may be operating without any Food Analysts. This is a sorry state of affair 
and speaks volumes of the inadequate technical competence of the FTLs in the country. 
The Committee would like FSSAI to urgently take up the matter of increasing the 
number of personnel in the laboratory with the States. The Committee underlines an 
urgent need for the States/UTs to  work in close partnership with FSSAI for ensuring a 
better food safety mechanism in the country. The Committee further urges the 
States/UTs to follow the guidance document for setting up a food testing laboratory. 
(Para 3.97) 
 
 The Committee has taken cog nizance of the progress made in regard to 
implementation of the Central Sector Schemes for 'Strengthening of Food Testing 
System' in the country.  It finds that out of a total outlay of Rs. 481.95 crore, a sum of 
Rs. 312.98 crore has been sanctioned/releas ed to States/UTs, while substantial balance 
amount to the tune of Rs. 168.97 crore still remained unspent as some of proposals are 
still under consideration. Non-utilisation of 35% funds and that too for a Central sector 
projects does not augur well and le aves a quantum made on the fixed management of 
the Ministry. 
(Para 3.103) 
 
STRENGTHENING OF STATE FOOD TESTING LABORATORIES (SFTLs) 
 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that out of the total target of upgrading 42 
SFTLS, upgradation of 39 SFTLS spread over 29 States/UTs have been taken up.  The 
Committee desires that upgradation of the remaining 3 labs may also be started at the 
earliest.  
(Para 3.104) 
 
 Notwithstanding the fact that the Committee has been emphasizing on the need 
of recruitment of Food Analysts in the country, there has been no perceptible change in 
the situation. The Committee, therefore, recommends FSSAI to expedite the 
recruitment of Food Analysts in the country and also take up the matter with the State 
Governments. Special attention should also be paid on the qualification of the Food 
Analyst so that only technically qualified and experienced personnel are recruited on 
the post of Food  Analysts. There is also a need to develop a monitoring mechanism for 
the work done by Food Analysts so that they are not tempted into giving false reports.  
 
(Para 3.108) 
FOOD SAFETY ON WHEELS (FSW) 
 
 The Committee notes the potential of mobile food testi ng laboratories, Food 
Safety on Wheels (FSWs) and recommends FSSAI to upgrade and increase the number 
of FSWs especially in remote areas. The Committee reiterates its recommendation on 
utilising the rich demographic dividend of the country and urges FSSAI to conduct 
extensive training program for the youth. The Committee strongly recommends FSSAI 

89 
 
to devise a special training program for the youth for operating these mobile testing 
labs.   
(Para 3.114) 
 
 The Committee feels that awareness on food safety and quality provisions and 
implication of FSS Act and its regulation is still lacking. The Committee understands 
that the massive outreach programme of FSSAI viz. 'Eat Right India' Swasth Bharat 
Yatra etc. would go a  long way in spreading awareness about the provisions of the 
FSSAI and its regulation.  The Committee, therefore, feels that a lot more needs to be 
done by FSSAI on these fronts. 
(Para 3.120) 
REGULATION OF FOOD ITEMS 
 
 The Committee notes the provisions of proposed amendments in Section 59 A in 
the Food Safety and Standard Act, 2006 intended to curb the rampant adulteration of 
the food products and the penal provision thereon. The Committee, however, 
recommends the Minis try to expedite the process of the proposed amendments so that 
the growing menace of adulteration of milk and dairy products having serious health 
implication is combated in right earnest.  
(Para 3.123) 
 
REGULATION OF PRESERVATIVES/CHECMICALS USED FOR STOR AGE FOR 
FISHES, ARTIFICIAL RIPENING OF FRUITS/VEGETABLES AND EDIBLE ICE 
 
 Taking note of rampant sale of loose edible oil in village and remote towns, the 
Committee recommends FSSAI to take up the issue with States and UTs Government. 
Keeping in view the need of economically weaker section of the society, edible oil 
companies ha s appropriately been allowed to make edible oil available in small 
pouches/sachets. The Committee, nevertheless, recommends FSSAI to carry out regular 
inspection in FBOs where large scale oil is consumed especially in shops where the 
leftover cooking oil i s being used multiple times. The Committee is of the view that the 
FSSAI should conduct regular training for acquainting the FBOs about the safe 
disposal of the oil and understand how repeated heating of the oil dangerously changes 
the fatty acid composition of the oil.  
(Para 3.130) 
PLASTIC IN FOOD ITEMS/WATER 
 
 The Committee observes that many street food stalls keep selling fried food 
reusing the same oil. The Committee understands that FSSAI has issued regulation on 
limit for TPC to a maximum of 25% beyond which the cooking oil is unsafe for 
consumption.  The Committee, therefore, recommends FSSAI to conduct on the spot 
inspection in food stalls to ensure the permissible 25% limit for Total Polar Compounds 
(TPC) is not crossed and penal action taken a gainst those defaulting FBOs. Moreover, 
the Committee is of the view that mere issuance of advisory is not the solution and 
FSSAI will have to take more pro -active steps to facilitate the mandatory inclusion of 
street food vendors in this initiative. 
(Para 3.134) 
 
 
 

90 
 
REGULATION OF GENETICALLY MODIFIED (GM) FOODS 
 
 The Committee in its 110 th Report had raised concerns over the snail pace of 
drafting of regulations and guidelines with respect to the labelling norms, safety 
assessment of food derived by GM technology etc.  The Committee is disappointed to 
note that even after two years of the p resentation of this Report, the regulations have 
not been notified. The Committee, therefore, strongly urges upon the Ministry to 
expedite the process of notification of Regulation on GM foods so that the import of 
food products is regulated and every food  product with a GM ingredient is inspected. 
The Committee seeks to be informed about the strategy chalked out for making public 
awareness campaign by FSSAI on the concept and constitution of GM Foods and its 
implication.  
(Para 3.140) 
 
REGULATION OF IMPORTED FOOD ITEMS 
 
 The Committee observes that the data submitted by the Ministry is outdated as 
the same pertains to the year 2016 -17. The Committee recommends the Ministry to 
submit latest data regarding clearance of imported food through different points o f 
entry being handled by FSSAI and other points of entry which are being handled by 
customs.   
(Para 3.143) 
REGULATION OF ORGANIC FOOD 
 
 The Committee appreciates that FSSAI understands the difficulties faced by 
small FBOs in accessing the market. The Committee, however, is quite apprehensive of 
the proposal for inclusion of a provision for "aggregator/ intermediary" in the FSS 
(Organic Foods) Regulations, 2017.  The Committee, in this regard, recommends that 
FSSAI should take necessary measures to ensu re that the small FBOs are not exploited 
and get adequate remuneration of their produce. 
 
(Para 3.149) 
REGULATION OF FORTIFIED FOOD 
 
 The Committee recommends that the observation/message, enshrined in the 
report titled “Food Fortification in India: Status and Road Ahead - Need for a Strategic 
Shift for Further Scale Up” detailing State best practices and supply chain models of 
Select states, be implemented by other States. The Committee believes that the children 
benefitted under two cherished programmes of the country viz. Mid -Day Meal (MDM) 
and Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS) would be beneficiary of fortified 
foods.  
(Para 3.152) 
 
REGULATION OF FOOD IN EATERIES 
 
 The Committee desires that the proposed amendments in FSS (Packaging &  
Labelling) Regulation with regard to display of information in food service 
establishment be notified without delay. The Committee also recommends that apart 
from display of information relating to calorific value of food and nutritive value of 
food in th e menu, quantity of portion should also be specified in the menu. The 
Committee also reiterates its recommendation for periodic inspection of basic 

91 
 
infrastructure of food service establishment and the adoption of standard hygiene 
practices therein.    
(Para 3.155) 
PACKAGING 
 
 The Committee recommends FSSAI to escalate its efforts in implementing food 
safety norms and guidelines in view of the outbreak of pandemic Covid -19 and 
thereafter in the wake of unlocking Phase. The Committee further recommends FSSAI 
to collaborate with different groups of street vendors and FBOs and increase the reach 
of its digital training program on hygiene issues for ensuing food safety standards 
during this peculiar phase. The Committee opines that the need of the hour is to draw  
area specific programs for street food vendors and strict adherence to safety practices 
such as using disinfectant, wearing protective gears, maintaining social distancing etc. 
in the FBO premises.  
(Para 3.158) 
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendati on that FSSAI should create a food 
advertising monitoring cell to monitor all the food advertisements and disseminate the 
information regarding misleading advertisements to the public. 
 
(Para 3.166) 
 
 The Committee takes note of a dedicated interaction portal for making food 
purchasers into smart, alert and aware consumers. The Committee would like the 
FSSAI to take certain initiatives for spreading awareness among the rural consumers 
too since these co nsumers may face difficulty in accessing the FSSAI portal and a 
helpline number instead would certainly give voice to their complaints.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends to FSSAI to have dedicated helpline number for addressing the 
complaints of such consumers.  
(Para 3.170) 
INFORMATION EDUCATION COMMUNICATION (IEC) 
 
 The Committee notes the FSSAI's initiative in digitising the different aspects of 
food safety infrastructure and record management to ensure not only better data 
management and easy accessibility but also transparency in food business management.  
Nevertheless, considering the low level of digital literacy in the country, the Committee 
recommends FSSAI to also ensure that the FBOs get the required capacity and training 
to access these platforms. 
(Para 3.174)

taken from those areas. 
National Milk Safety and Standards Survey, 
2018 has provided a comprehensive view milk 
quality ain over 1100 cities and towns covering  
all States / UTs. Based on this, risk -based 
surveillance and monitoring in identified hot 
spots would be taken up with the support of State 
Food Authorities.   
4) State Food Safety Authorities should also ensure that 
there is adequate lab testing infrastructure and ensure 
that all labs have/obtain NABL accreditation to 
facilitate precise testing. State Government to ensure 
that State food testing laboratories/district food 
laboratories are well -equipped with the technical 
persons and testing facilities. 
 
 
 
 
By notifying 172 food -testing laboratories 19 
referral laboratories for primary testing and 
appellate testing respectively, FSSAI has created 
a nation -wide network of food testing 
laboratories in the country that includes testing 
of milk and milk products. 
Further, States/UTs are being supported to 
upgrade their own food testing laboratories so 
that these adequately equipped with necessary 
technical persons and testing facilities including 
comprehensive testing of quality parameters, 
contaminants and adulterant in milk and milk 
products. So far, 29 State labsin 25 States/UTs 
have been supported.  
5) Special measures should be undertaken by the State 
Food Safety Authorities (SFSA) and District 
Authorities for sampling of milk and milk products, 
including spot testing through Mobile Food Testing 
Vans equipped with primary testing kits for conducting 
qualitative test of adulteration in food. 
FSSAI is providing mobile food testing vans labs 
and EMAT machines to State Food Safety 
Authorities (SFSA) for spo t testing of milk and 
conduct of basic quantitative tests to assess 
adulteration of milk. So far, 32 mobile food 
testing vans to 27 States/UTs  have been 
provided. In addition, EMAT (Electronic Milk 
Adulteration Tester) has also been to 29 
State/UTs.  
6) Since the snap short survey conducted in 2011 revealed 
adulteration of milk by hazardous substances including 
chemicals, such snap short surveys to be conducted 
periodically both in the State as well as at the national 
level by FSSAI. 
While, in case of raw mil k, States / UTs would 
be advised to carry out snapshot surveys, for 
processed milk, a system of regular monitoring 
of milk quality is being put in place, wherein 
milk quality and safety would be checked 
periodically for all milk processing plants with 
periodicity calibrated based on tracking of test 
results.   

99 
 
 
7) For curbing milk adulteration, an appropriate State 
level Committee headed by the Chief Secretary or the 
Secretary of Dairy Department and District level 
Committee headed by the concerned District C ollector 
shall be constituted as is done in the State of 
Maharashtra to take the review of the work done to 
curb the milk adulteration in the district and in the State 
by the authorities. 
Review of activities taken up in the States/UTs 
and Districts has be en included in the terms of 
reference of the State Advisory Committee for 
food safety and nutrition and District level 
Committeefor food safety and nutrition headed 
by the Chief Secretary and District Magistrate 
respectively. For this specific purpose, the y have 
been advised to set up a sub -committee of 
stakeholders, if required for closer monitoring.  
8) To prevent adulteration of milk, the concerned State 
Department shall set up a website thereby specifying 
the functioning and responsibilities of food safety 
authorities and also creating awareness about complaint 
mechanisms. In the website, the contact details of the 
Joint Commissioners including the Food Safety 
Commissioners shall be made available for registering 
the complaints on the said website. Al l States should 
also have and maintain toll free telephonic and online 
complaint mechanism. 
FSSAI has created a website for monitoring 
quality and safety of milk in the country with 
details of complaint handling system for each 
State. States have also been advised to strengthen 
their complaint handling system.   
9) In order to increase consumer awareness about ill 
effects of milk adulteration as stipulated in  Section 
18(1)(f) the State  Food Authority/Commissioner of 
Food Safety shall inform the general public  of the 
nature of risk to health and create awareness of food 
safety and standards. They should also educate school 
children by conducting workshops and teaching them 
easy methods for detection of common adulterants in 
food, keeping in mind indigenous tech nological 
innovations (such as milk adulteration detection strips 
etc.)  
A series of steps have been taken for consumer 
awareness across the country with special focus 
on school children. This is also an important of 
the Eat Right India movement taken up. This 
includes organising of Eat Right Melas, Food 
Safety Magic Box for testing of common 
adulterants and booklet for detection of 
adulterants (including in milk) through rapid 
testing (DART).  
10) Union of India/State Governments to evolve a 
complaint mechani sm for checking corruption and 
other unethical practices of the Food Authorities and 
their officers. 
FSSAI has created a code of ethics for field level 
food safety officials. States have been advised to 
develop effective systems to address complaints 
of co rruption and unethical behaviour of food 
safety officials.

 Annexure 4 
S.N. Recommendations Follow up action required 
1. Monitoring of compliance of food testing 
by FBOs for optimal utilization of 
laboratories capacity - through 
INFOLNET/3rd party  
Presently, laboratories are being connected on to the 
INFOLNET which will be followed by FSOs and FBOs (for 
now link for FBOs to access is not available on 
INFOLNET) 
2. Creation of a national lab advisory 
committee for guiding FSSAI on issues 
related to food testing labs  
It is being considered 
3. Ensuring availability of adequate number 
of qualified staff especially food analy st 
and their training on safety parameters 
(like pesticides and heavy metal)  
Recruitment of staff is the prerogative of States/UTs. The 
matter has been raised with them a number of times in CAC 
meeting, VCs, letters etc. and they are being on regular basis. 
Further, there are adequate numbers of Food/Public Analysts 
in India. 
Apart from organizing specialized trainings on safety 
parameters (like pesticides, veterinary drugs including 
antibiotics, mycotoxins, etc), FSSAI has also established 
training ce ntres at Mumbai (called International Training 
Center on Food Safety & Applied Nutrition in association 
with EIC and GFSP) and at Ghaziabad to train on safety 
parameters (called Food Safety Solution Center in association 
with M/s Thermo Fisher; and, Center  for Microbiological 
Analysis Training in association with M/s Merck). These 
centres will be epicentres of capacity building for food 
analysts, especially in the government sector.  
4. Development of uniform sampling and 
supervision framework 
The work is being carried out by the Panel and method review 
group on priority.  
5. Creation of training centres for Hands on 
Training 
As mentioned above, ITC -FSAN at Mumbai and two training 
Centres created at the NFL, Ghaziabad have already been 
created for achieving the goal of hands on training. 
6. Organising national level awareness 
generation program with stakeholders to 
push testing demand by consumers 
FSSAI has provided mobile food testing laboratories called 
Food Safety on Wheels (FSW) which has options for t esting, 
awareness and training. 43 FSWs are in place in different 
States/UTs. These FSWs have been undertaking activities to 
create awareness amongst common citizenry about 
importance of food testing and eating safe.   
7. Drawing an Action Plan in coordin ation 
with State/UT Governments for 
overcoming the shortage of manpower of 
Food Regulatory Bodies. 
General norms are already in place as far as fulfilling the 
shortage FSOs and DOs across the States/UTs.  
As regards to laboratory staff, a Guidance Document  on 
setting up of FTLs has already been shared with States/UTs 
and is available on the website of FSSAI. This document 
gives  a general guideline in regards to the number of staff 
required in a state food testing laboratory. 
8. Delegation of financial powers to state 
laboratories for smooth operation of labs 
on regular basis 
This needs to be done by the State governments. Also, the 
matter has been raised with States/UTs a number of times 
during CAC meetings, video conferences with States and 
during the visit of FSSAI officials to different States/UTs.  
9. Establishment of a separate agency or 
department of Food Safety in each State 
for better enforcement  
This needs to be done by the State governments. 
10. Formation of a cerntralized pool of 
vendors an d equipment service providers 
for the convenience of labs 
FSSAI has empanelled vendors for a few high end equipment. 
The Government e -Market (GeM) portal has provision for 
sourcing equipment, consumables and services. 
11. Providing grant by MoFPI only to 
NABL/FSSAI recognized laboratories  
This relates to MoFPI.  
12. Establishment of Single Window System 
(SWS) instead of multiple accreditation 
and recognition. 
Steps to this effect has  already been taken and an integrated 
audit system for accreditation and recognition of food testing 
laboratories has become operational with FSSAI being part of 
it, since April 2019.

III. NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.8 The Committee would also like to emphasize that India is known to be a treasure trove of 
medicinal plants. What is required is to identify, conserve and gratefully use them for medicinal 
purposes. Theref ore, focus of the Board should be on utilizing the rich biodiversity on a 
sustainable basis. The Committee would also like to highlight the pivotal role that the local 
community can play in development, conservation and sustainable use of such plants. The 
Committee, in this regard, recommends the NMPB to popularize a programme for sustainable 
development of Medicinal Plants amongst the local community. 
(Para 3.13) 
Action Taken 
 
1.9 For Sustainable Development of medicinal Plants amongst the local communitie s (Joint 
Forest Management Committees (JFMCs)/Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs), 
Panchayats/Van Panchayats etc.), there is a provision under “Central Sector Scheme on 
Conservation, Development and Sustainable Management of Medicinal Plants” of NMPB .  As 
per the said scheme guidelines financial assistance of Rs.15.00 Lakh per JFMCs/BMCs etc. is 
provided for creation of primary processing facilities in the form of Drying   Yards, Storage 
Godowns etc. for value addition of medicinal plants raw material and thereby generating 
livelihood to the local communities. 
  
1.10 Under “Central Sector Scheme on Conservation, Development and Sustainable 
Development of Medicinal Plants”, National Medicinal Plant Board supports for Medicinal Plants 
Conservation Areas (MPCDAs) and resource augmentation as project mode.   MPCDAs cover on 
an average area of 200 hectares or smaller areas in case of endemic and critically endangered 
species.  As per guideline, financial assistance of @20,000 per hectare is provided. 
  
1.11 In addition, resource augmentation of medicinal plant species assisted through natural 
regeneration and artificial regeneration of local populations of medicinal and aromatic plant.   
Active interest and engagement of rural communities in such a conservation program is 
instrumental to address sustainability of the medicinal plant sector as a whole, hence financial 
support also provided for community mobilization through entry point activities etc. 
  
1.12 Under “Central Sector Scheme on Conservation, Developmen t and Sustainable 
development of Medicinal Plants”, under which there is a provision to provide project based 
support to various Government and Non -Government organizations to establish various types of 
herbal garden to popularize the usefulness of commonl y available and frequently used Medicinal 
Plants among the various stakeholders and sensitize the public about our traditional knowledge. It 
is also a way of conserving Rare, Endangered and Threatened (RET) species of Medicinal 
Plants.  Setting up of Herba l Gardens are promoted under the scheme to create awareness about 
traditional usage of medicinal plants.

IV.  QUALITY CONTROL OF AYURVEDA, SIDDHA, UNANI AND 
HOMOEOPATHIC (AYUSH) DRUGS 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.13 The Committee time and again has been emphasizin g upon a stringent regulatory 
framework for quality control of ASU&H drugs. The Committee believes that for AYUSH 
systems to emerge as a strong alternative system of medicine, it is imperative that its credibility is 
enhanced through proper monitoring, qua lity control of drugs by scientific validation, proper 
parameters for clinical trials, upgradation of drug testing labs, GMP compliance by manufacturing 
units, control of misleading advertisements, etc. The Committee taking note of all the 
achievements would like to recommend that quality control of ASU&H drugs is one of the most 
important areas within the AYUSH ambit which needs to be accorded utmost priority. There is 
also a need for integration of AYUSH system of medicine with the modern system which is only 
possible through scientific validation and strict quality control for safety and efficacy of this 
system of medicine. The Committee strongly recommends for expediting and bringing forth the 
legislation for a regulatory umbrella for the education and p rofession of Pharmacy in Indian 
Medicine and Homoeopathy.   
(Para 4.4) 
Action Taken 
 
1.14 The Ministry has taken note of the recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee and 
would like to inform that Pharmacopoeia Commission of Indian Medicine and Homeopathy, 
Pharmacopoeia Laboratory of Indian Medicine and Homeopathic Pharmacopoeia Laboratory 
have been set up. These organisations are mandated to develop the quality standards of Ayurveda, 
Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy (ASU&H) Drugs and publish the Pharmacopoeia.  
Pharmacopoeia are the regulatory document for the purpose of quality control of ASU&H drugs.  
  
1.15 The Cabinet in its meeting held on 03.06.2020 has approved the establishment of 
PCIM&H as subordinate office under Ministry of AYUSH by merging PLIM & HPL  both 
subordinate offices and PCIM&H an autonomous organization under Ministry of AYUSH. 
 
1.16 Similarly, the setting up of the regulatory framework through Pharmacy Council of Indian 
Medicine and Homoeopathy Bill, 2020 is being steered for approval of the  Cabinet and thereafter 
introduction of the same in the Parliament.   
 
 
V. PHARMA COVIGILENCE INITIATIVES FOR ASU DRUGS 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.17 The Committee observes that a very low amount of allocation is being made for the scheme 
bearing a very vital mand ate. Even though the utilization of this paltry allocation is not quite 
satisfactory, the Committee is of the view that adequate and an enhanced allocation for this scheme 
is essential to create a strong Pharmacovigilance network across the country so as t o ensure 
effective control of misleading advertisements, safety monitoring of ASU&H drugs, 
documentations and analysis of Adverse Drug Reactions, etc. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends sufficient enhancement of funds for the scheme at RE stage. 
(Para 5.3)

1.18 The network of Pharmacovigilance centres of ASU&H drugs is getting established and 
more peripheral pharmacovigilance centres have been added to the network. Accordingly, the 
recommendations of the Hon'ble Parliamentary Committee has b een noted and   provision of Rs. 
2.83 crore has been made in the B.E. 2020 -21, which can be appropriately enhanced in 
accordance with the proposal of requirement of funds from Pharmacovigilance Centres.   
 
Recommendation 
 
1.19 The Committee noting the vario us initiatives being taken under the scheme of 
Pharmacovigilance initiatives, observes that the Ministry is in the process of building a 
network/structure for carrying out strict monitoring/vigilance of quality control of ASU&H drugs. 
The Committee feels that this 3-tier network of pharmacovigilance needs to play pro -active role in 
reporting adverse drug events along with surveillance of misleading advertisements. With the 
Steering & Monitoring Committee, Technical Advisory Committee and Central Signal Dete ction

the said scheme, the Committee hopes that the task relating to the well -being of patients 
consuming ASU&H drugs will be taken care of. The Committee emp hasizes upon the need for 
imparting training and capacity building and also the awareness generation of ASU&H 
Pharmacovigilance so as to educate all involved in the network of pharmacovigilance for 
successful implementation of the scheme. 
(Para 5.5)

awareness, three (3) CME training programs were conducted by the Intermediary

been conducted by the Peripheral Pharmacovigilance Centres to develop better understanding

II.  BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.1 The Committee is disappointed to note that against the projected demand of Rs. 5035.27 
crore for 2020-21, the Ministry of AYUSH has been allocated Rs. 2122.08 crores reflecting huge 
shortfall of Rs. 2913.19 crores. The budgetary estimates of 2020 -21 when compared with RE 
2019-20 indicate a marginal increase of Rs. 265.08 crores only for the Ministry. The Committ ee 
appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry to get enhanced allocation but could not succeed. The 
Committee is constrained to note that several schemes of the Ministry would be affected due to 
shortfall of funds. The Committee apprehends that the objec tives of important schemes like 
National Ayush Mission, Health and Wellness centres etc would not be fulfilled due to financial 
constraints. Moreover, several research projects, construction work of National Institutes and 
Research Councils would also get affected. The Committee takes note of submission of the 
Ministry to make up the shortfall of funds by seeking a loan of Rs.1000 crore from Higher 
Education Funding Agency (HEFA), to support, in particular, the 8 construction projects of 
National Institutes. The Committee is surprised to note that financial constraints have forced the 
Ministry to raise loan which shows that Government is not very serious towards promoting 
AYUSH and letting it emerge as an alternative and economical system of medicine. The 
Committee, however, is of the view that that the Ministry, being a relatively new one requires 
adequate funds and resources for proving its efficacy and worth. The Committee, in its previous 
Reports, has consistently been emphasizing upon substantial increas e in the allocation to the 
Ministry for executing its various schemes/programmes. The Committee, therefore, strongly, 
recommends the Ministry to approach Ministry of Finance at RE stage with the request for 
additional demand so that implementations of sche mes of the Ministry are not affected, adversely. 
It also recommends to the Ministry to utilize the allocated funds optimally with focus on the 
priority areas and make best use of the available funds. 
(Para 2.4) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.2 It is a fact that this Min istry has been allocated an amount of Rs. 2,122.08 crore for the 
year 2020-21 as against the projected demand of Rs. 5,025.37 crore, which is only 3.26 per cent 
of the Health Budget.   Apart from the above, this Ministry has already moved a proposal to 
obtain a loan of Rs.1,000.00 crore from Higher Education Finance Agency (HEFA) to augment 
fund for the work projects being undertaken by the various National Institutes functioning under 
this Ministry.   The proposal is under the active consideration at the app ropriate level in the 
Ministry of Finance.  Since the allocation was less than the projected requirements, this Ministry 
had taken up the matter immediately on receipt of the allocation with senior level officers of the 
Ministry of Finance including the Fi nance Minister to apprise them of the inadequacy of Budget 
allocation vis-à-vis the projection.  Further, as recommended by the Committee, this Ministry will 
also take up the issue again at the RE stage for increasing the allocation.  Further, the endeavour  
and efforts of this Ministry is to utilize the funds allotted optimally, but in some cases the 

10 
 
utilization could not be achieved due to non -approval/late approval of some schemes during the 
year despite best efforts put in by the Ministry. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.3 The Committee is of the considered view that lower budgetary allocation (Rs.2,122.08 
crores) against the projected demand of (Rs.5025.21 crore) in BE 2020 -21 would not make the 
Ministry capable of achieving its mandate to develop AYUSH System  as the preferred system of 
living and practice for attaining a healthy India.  The Committee had in its 108th Report 
recommended that at least 5% of the total health b udget should be allocated to the Ministry of 
AYUSH. However, the actual allocation remai ned at 3.26%, as a result of which the physical 
performance of various construction projects and schemes viz. National AYUSH Mission Health 
and Wellness centre viz -a-viz originally conceived plan would definitely suffer.  The Ministry is 
now compelled to m eet the shortfall of funds by seeking a loan of Rs. 1000 crores from Higher 
Education Funding Agency to support the 8 construction projects of National Institutes and on -
going schemes.  
 
3.4 The Committee, however, would  also like to be apprised of the sta tus of loan of Rs.1000 
crore from Higher Education Finance Agency (HEFA) and the response of the Ministry of 
Finance to the request of Ministry of AYUSH for higher allocation at RE Stage keeping in view 
the inadequacy of budgetary allocation viz -a-viz  pro jected demand at RE Stage.   The 
Committee would also like to be informed of the final appropriation of allocated budget, viz -a-
viz projected allocation at RE Stage on various Schemes of the Ministry and the status note on 
the physical achievement of vario us schemes due to lower budgetary allocation.  Such s tatus 
note should also reflect the actual physical achievement against the objective set under various 
schemes at the time of projecting demand at BE Stage.   Given the imminent need for higher 
allocation of funds to the Ministry, the Committee reiterates its recommendation of allocating at 
least 5% of the total Health Budget for the Ministry of AYUSH. 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.5  The Committee notes a difference of Rs. 1693.3 crore in the projected demand of Rs.  
4469.59 crore in BE 2019-20 and the demand of Rs. 2776.29 crore at the RE stage. This, according 
to the Committee, speaks volumes not only about the paradigms shift in its original conceived 
schemes but also utilization capacity of the Ministry. The Commi ttee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry must make realistic assessment of its fund requirement keeping in view on -going 
projects/projects to be undertaken and accordingly project its demand. 
(Para 2.5) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.6 With regard to less projectio n of funds at RE Stage as compared to the BE stage, it may 
be mentioned that the projection made in Budget Estimates are generally made keeping in view 
the prospective plan and execution of the projects during the course of the entire financial year, 
whereas while projecting the requirement at RE stage it is purely based on the actual balance 
work/requirement to be carried out during the remaining period of the Financial Year keeping in 
mind the scope of   utilization of fund allotted in RE which  are generally made available to the 
Programme Divisions  in the fag end of the Financial Year after due process of formalities such 

11 
 
as obtaining of supplementary grant and issue of re -appropriation orders etc.. Therefore, the 
projection of the requirement at RE stage  is made which is more realistic vis -à-vis availability of 
fund and time. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.7 The Committee is not convinced with Ministry's response  that projection  made at BE 
stage is generally made keeping in view the prospective plan and the progress made in 
execution of projects during the entire financial year. The Committee believes that the 
ambitious and lofty plans of the Ministry must be commensurate to its capacity to utilize the 
funds optimally and therefore, the projection should not be far -fetched and unrealistic .  In 
fact, realistic assessment of what can actually be achieved and spent in one financial year 
should be done.  The Committee,  therefore, is of the view that the Ministry should be more 
cautious and grounded in its financial projections. 
 
3.8 The Committee, at the same time, is constrained to observe that the Ministry of AYUSH 
falls short of the target of optimum utilization of allocated funds due to non -approval /late 
approval of some Schemes.  This argument speaks poorly about the state of affairs in terms of 
the decision making process and monitoring capacity of the Ministry. The Committee, in this 
regard, observes that all the formalities/procedures viz., obtaining supplementary demands and 
issuance of re -appropriation or der must be completed without waiting for the fag -end of the 
financial year. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends for timely approval of schemes 
as well as timely release of fund for ensuring completion of projects within scheduled time and 
without cost over-run.   
 
Recommendation 
 
3.9 The Committee observes that the reasons for under-utilization of allocated funds are mainly 
administrative which could have easily been avoided had there been proper prudential monitoring 
and supervision during execu tion of the on -going projects/schemes. The Committee is of the firm 
view that proper co -ordination and financial controlling needs to be spearheaded on all the 
construction activities undertaken so that funds are not left idle due to delays in construction  
causing time as well as cost overruns. Similarly, filing up of vacant posts in all the institutes/bodies 
under the Ministry should be accorded priority. Also, delay or non -receipt of adequate proposals 
from stakeholders especially States/UTs for any schem e indicates that the scheme needs to be

all the schemes so that the  physical as well financial targets of various schemes as set in Output -
Outcome Statement are accomplished.

Further Recommendation 
 
3.52 The Committee finds a grim picture o f filled as well as vacant posts in this Institute. Out 
of 22 sanctioned posts, only 5 have been filled up. The Committee would like to highlight  that 
the Institute is mandated to create an interface between traditional/folk medical practitioner and 
research. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that all the sanctioned posts 
(except posts sub -judice) should be filled up as early as possible so that the Institute is able to 
function properly, thereby ensuring optimum utilization of allocated budgetary fund.

VII. RESEARCH COUNCILS 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.1 The Committee is anguished to note such a low allocation of budget to the R esearch 
Councils as compared to their projected demand. Which Government is attempting to mainstream 
AYUSH systems of medicine on the one hand, such a low allocation to Research Councils on the 
other will not only restrict the research activities in these councils but would further hinder the 
development of AYUSH services within the country. The Committee is of the view that Research 
is an ongoing activity and is a long drawn process requiring adequate funds. These Research 
Councils certainly need adequate budgetary support for continuing their researches and also to 
promote more and more research activities/projects. The Committee would also like to highlight 
that tangible outcomes of these researches would incentivize the students at large willing to opt f or 
Indian system of medicine. Keeping this in mind, the Committee is of the firm view that the 
allocation of budget to these Councils should be enhanced. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends the Ministry to persuade Ministry of Finance for the higher all ocation of Budgetary 
provision at the RE stage.

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.4 The Committee is constrained to observe that the amount of allocation for the Ministry of

of the view that in order to explore the full potential of Ayush systems, it is imperative to allocate

Recommendation

28 
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS — AT A GLANCE 
 
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
 The Committee is of the considered view that lower budgetary allocation (Rs.2,122.08 
crores) against the projected demand of (Rs.5025.21 crore) in BE 2020 -21 would not make 
the Ministry capable of achieving its mandate to develop AYUSH System as the preferred 
system of living and practice for attaining a healthy India.  The Co mmittee had in its 108 th 
Report recommended that at least 5% of the total health budget should be allocated to the 
Ministry of AYUSH. However, the actual allocation remained at 3.26%, as a result of which 
the physical performance of various construction projects and schemes viz. National AYUSH 
Mission Health and Wellness centre viz -a-viz originally conceived plan would definitely 
suffer.  The Ministry is now compelled to meet the shortfall of funds by seeking a loan of Rs. 
1000 crores from Higher Education Funding Agency to support the 8 construction projects 
of National Institutes and on-going schemes.  
(Para 3.3) 
 
 The Committee, however, would also like to be apprised of the status of loan of 
Rs.1000 crore from Higher Education Finance Agency (HEFA) and t he response of the 
Ministry of Finance to the request of Ministry of AYUSH for higher allocation at RE Stage 
keeping in view the inadequacy of budgetary allocation viz -a-viz  projected demand at RE 
Stage.   The Committee would also like to be informed of t he final appropriation of allocated 
budget, viz-a-viz projected allocation at RE Stage on various Schemes of the Ministry and 
the status note on the physical achievement of various schemes due to lower budgetary 
allocation.  Such status note should also re flect the actual physical achievement against the 
objective set under various schemes at the time of projecting demand at BE Stage.  Given the 
imminent need for higher allocation of funds to the Ministry, the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation of allo cating at least 5% of the total Health Budget for the Ministry of 
AYUSH. 
(Para 3.4) 
 
 The Committee is not convinced with Ministry's response that projection  made at 
BE stage is generally made keeping in view the prospective plan and the progress made in 
execution of projects during the entire financial year. The Committee believes that the 
ambitious and lofty plans of the Ministry must be commensurate to its capacity to utilize 
the funds optimally and therefore, the projection should not be far -fetched and unrealistic.  
In fact, realistic assessment of what can actually be achieved and spent in one financial year 
should be done.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the Ministry should be more 
cautious and grounded in its financial projections. 
(Para 3.7) 
 

29 
 
 The Committee, at the same time, is constrained to observe that the Ministry of 
AYUSH falls short of the target of optimum utilization of allocated funds due to non -
approval /late approval of some Schemes.  This argument speaks poorly about the state of 
affairs in terms of the decision making process and monitoring capacity of the Ministry. 
The Committee, in this regard, observes that all the formalities/procedures viz., obtaining 
supplementary demands and issuance of re-appropriation order must be completed without 
waiting for the fag -end of the financial year. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends for timely approval of schemes as well as timely release of fund for ensuring 
completion of projects within scheduled time and without cost over-run.   
(Para 3.8) 
 
 The Committee is perturbed to note that incapacity to utilize allocated funds by 
AIIA, New Delhi has resulted into unspent balance amount to the tune of Rs. 13.73 crore 
and that too under capital head.  The Committee has always laid stress on the removal of 
administrative or procedural constraints that cause delay in implementation of the various 
schemes of the Ministry.  Time and again, the Committee has emphasized upon effective 
monitoring of construction activity to avoid time and cost over -runs.  The Committee 
expresses its deep concern over in -ordinate delay in filling up the vacant posts in various 
Institutes and research organizations under the administrative jurisdiction of the Ministry 
of AYUSH. The Committee would like the Mi nistry to ensure timely completion of the 
recruitment process for manpower in NMPB, NEIAH, Shillong, NIA, Jaipur, NIS, Chennai, 
NEIFM, Passighat, CCRAS, CCRS.  The Committee expects the Ministry to be more 
dynamic and pro -active in discharging its duties a nd responsibilities in an efficient and 
effective manner and to realize the objective of proper development of AYUSH systems of 
medicine.    
(Para 3.14) 
 
 The Committee finds the response of the Ministry quite evasive with regard to their 
efforts towards l iquidation of Utilization Certificate from States/ UTs. Merely sharing the 
figure of 1222 pending cases involving Rs.1093.45 crores as on 31.01.2020 does not give the 
right picture of pendency of UCs.  In fact, the same status was obtained at the time of t he 
presentation of 120th Report on the Demands for Grants (2020 -21).  The Action Taken Notes 
should have reflected the updated status of UCs after the presentation of the said report. 
This amounts to lackadaisical approach towards implementation of the rec ommendation of 
the Committee. 
(Para 3.17) 
 
 The Committee is distressed to note that the dedicated web portal for Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme of ‘National AYUSH Mission’, concerning submission of Utilisation 
Certificate is still languishing at development s tage.  In a nutshell, the necessary action, on 
the part of the Ministry, leaves too much to be desired. The Committee strongly believes that 
inordinate delay in operationalization of the portal is a matter of concern.  In this IT era, 
inability to initiate and make use of technology is unacceptable. The Committee desires that 

30 
 
pendency of UCs involving a huge sum of Rs. 1093.45 crores needs to be taken up pro -
actively with all the States/UTs so that it does not hinder further release of funds thereby 
affecting the implementation of schemes. The Committee is optimistic that  
operationalization of the portal would definitely  facilitate the  timely submission of UCs.  
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends for finalisation of development of dedicated 
web-portal for Centrally Sponsored Scheme of National AYUSH Mission (NAM) without 
further procrastination so that the problem of pendency of UG is resolved at the earliest. 
 
(Para 3.18) 
 
 It is disheartening that the considerable number of UCs are pending for  NMPB and 
NAM. The Committee has been laying stress on focusing on liquidation of pending cases of 
UCs with respect to the two schemes of the Ministry i.e. NAM and National Medicinal  
Plants Board.  Pending cases of UCs is high for these two schemes involving huge amount of 
money. Since now NMPB/NAM have already set up a Monitoring Cell in the Account 
Division, the Committee hopes that this cell would  successfully be able to check the 
pendency of UCs which would ensure timely implementation of the schemes.  The 
Committee recommends the Ministry to evaluate the functioning of the Monitoring Cell 
with respect to liquidation of pending UCs after one year since its set up.  
(Para 3.23) 
 
III. NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD 
 
 The Committee notes the measures take n by the Ministry for liquidating pending 
UCs under Central Sector Scheme.  However, the Ministry has not apprised the Committee 
about the outcome of measures so undertaken i.e. extent of  to which the pending UCs cases 
and  the sum total of amount got imp acted.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry to apprise the Committee of impact of steps taken on the settlement of pending 
UCs under National Medical Plants Board. 
(Para 3.26) 
  
Given the vital objective of the scheme with respect to construc tion development and 
sustainable management of medicinal plants, it is the need of the hour to lay special focus 
on the scheme and especially on liquidation of pending UCs to avoid blockage of further 
release of funds for effective implementation of scheme.  
(Para 3.27) 
 
 The Committee is disdained to note that the issue of augmentation of human 
resources for NMPB is still not settled.  It is given to understand that the proposal for 
creation of 65 new posts has been revisited and reduced to 24 posts which is less than half of 
what was envisaged earlier.  Surprisingly, even this creation of 24 posts is yet to be 
finalized.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the reasons for such steep 
reduction in the number of posts to be created for NMPB.  Given  the inordinate delay in 

31 
 
creation of posts, the Committee is skeptical about the augmentation of human resources 
for NMPB in recent future.  It apprehends the effective implementation of the Central 
Sector Scheme on conservation, development and sustainabl e management of Medicinal 
plants by NMPB.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends for NMPB for 
streamlining its human resource planning for carrying out efficiently its functions.  The 
NMPB Committee must finalise its draft note to be given to SIU a nd the Ministry of 
AYUSH must take pro -active steps for allocating adequate manpower to NMPB for 
carrying out assigned responsibility of Medicinal plant and that has become all the more 
necessary in view of outbreak of COVID-19 and the need for its mitigation. 
(Para 3.31) 
 
 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry should lay special 
focus on this matter and complete the process of the creation of new posts within this 
financial year itself so that recruitment for the said posts is initiated at the earliest. 
 
(Para 3.32) 
 
 The Committee notes that the 36 State Medicinal Plants Boards (SMPBs) have been 
constituted under different States/UTs but unfortunately State Medicinal Plants Boards are 
facing financial as well as human resource con straints.  The Committee in its earlier reports 
has been emphasizing upon the need for reforming and revitalizing the SMPBs so as to re -
activate these Boards into robust bodies supporting the NMPB in carrying out its mandate.  
The strengthening of SMPBs as sumes significance in case the Ministry wants to make its 
mark as an exporter of precious herbs and promoting commercial cultivation of medicinal 
plants on a sustainable basis. The Committee, therefore, recommends that special attention 
needs to be given t o reforming SMPBs and also actively engaging the States/UTs in the 
process with the purpose of strengthening SMPBs.   
(Para 3.36) 
VI.       NATIONAL AYUSH MISSION (NAM) 
 
 The Committee understands that National AYUSH Mission (NAM) is the only 
centrally spo nsored flagship programme of the Ministry under National Health Mission.  
The Committee has constantly observed huge gap between the projected demand and the 
actual allocation of funds for NAM despite potential absorption capacity of the Scheme.  The 
Ministry, in its action taken note, has argued that shortfall of funds has adversely impacted 
the achievement of the physical target of the schemes to a great extent.  The Committee notes 
that the Scheme contains the vast range of activities, viz, provision for  cost-effective AYUSH 
services, upgradation of AYUSH educational institutions and pharmacies and drug testing; 
cultivation and integration of medicinal plants, export of value added items of medicinal 
plants and promote herbal industry.  The Committee unde rlines the promotion of herbal 
industry as an effective system of medicine to mitigate the spread of Covid -19. Keeping this 
fact in view, the Committee strongly recommends for adequate allocation of funds as per the 

32 
 
requirement of National AYUSH Mission fo r ensuring and encouraging AYUSH as an 
alternative system of medicine in the country as well as abroad. 
(Para 3.40) 
 
 The Committee appreciates that the Ministry has conducted various regional review 
meetings to take stock of the  physical and financial  progress of National AYUSH Mission 
and has also constituted two teams for conducting field visits to review the physical progress 
in the States/UTs through field visits from time to time.  The Committee, however, believes 
that the mandate goes much beyond the se review meetings and field visits as the constraints 
noticed therein need to be identified and addressed immediately. Further, attention of the 
Committee has also been drawn to a Mid -Term evaluation undertaken under NAM 
guidelines and recommendations of  the evaluating agency shared with NITI Aayog followed 
by a Third Party evaluation for Umbrella Centrally Sponsored Schemes, including NAM. 
The Committee, however, is disappointed that the Ministry has neither shared the 
findings/observations and recommend ations of the evaluating agency with the Committee 
nor apprised the Committee of the action taken on the recommendations received to address 
the key concern areas.  The Committee, therefore, would like to be apprised of the 
observations/recommendations of the evaluating agency and response thereto for effective  
monitoring and evaluation of NAM in future. 
(Para 3.45) 
 
 The Committee notes that the National Research Institute of Unani Medicine for Skin 
Disorders (NRIUMSD), Hyderabad is the only Institute tha t has been granted NABH 
accreditation and the application for NABH accreditation for most of the Institutes are still 
under process. The Committee finds that status of progress of seeking NABH accreditation 
does not seem to be encouraging.  The Committee, there, would like to be apprised by the 
Ministry about the average time taken by any Institute to obtain NABH Accreditation. The 
Committee is of the considered view that NABH accreditation would enable the research 
institute to have scientific and quality research, focusing on effectiveness of the clinical trial 
process, ensuring commitment to quality, accountability and ensuring public trust and 
confidence with emphasis on protocols, policies as per national/international standards for 
patient care, clinic al outcomes, continuous improvement and monitoring of its services. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendations contained in Para 7.9 of the 120 th 
Report that Research Councils/Institutes must obtain NABH accreditation, sooner the better.  
(Para 3.48) 
 
  The Committee finds a grim picture of filled as well as vacant posts in this Institute. 
Out of 22 sanctioned posts, only 5 have been filled up. The Committee would like to highlight 
that the Institute is mandated to create an interface between traditional/folk medical 
practitioner and research. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that all 
the sanctioned posts (except posts sub -judice) should be filled up as early as possible so that 
the Institute is able to function properly,  thereby ensuring optimum utilization of allocated 
budgetary fund. 
(Para 3.52)

PREFACE 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this One -Hundred Twenty Third Report on t he Outbreak of Pandemic Covid -19 
And its Management.   
 
2. The primary objective behind identifying the subject – “The Outbreak of Pandemic 
COVID-19 And its Management” by the Committee is to assess the response of the Government 
to contain and mitigate the unprecedented outbreak of Pandemic COVID -19. The purpose of the 
report is not to criticise the Government’s course of action in combating the Pandemic but to 
identify the implementation gaps during the course of executing its contingent plan. At the 
outset, the Committee appreciates the Government’s initiatives and management of COVID -19 
in a country of 1.3 billion people. The Committee in its wisdom has attempted to provide policy 
prescription to the Government to utilise the most adverse situation arising due to outbreak of the 
Pandemic in the history of the mankind as an opportunity for transformation of our health 
infrastructure to best global standards. The need of the hour is adequate investment for the 
development of infrastructure of the health sector with the intent of making provision for the best 
healthcare delivery system. There is also a trumpet call for assimilation of latest health 
technology, raising of skilled health cadre into the public health system. Equally important is to 
mainstreaming the AYUSH System and its integration with modern system of medicine for 
proper healthcare of the people of the country.

CHAPTER - 1 
ADMINISTRATIVE MANAGEMENT OF LOCKDOWN AND UNLOCKING 
Outbreak of the Virus 
 
1.1 According to WHO, the outbreak of febrile respiratory illness of unknown etiology in 
December, 2019 originated from Wuhan, Hubei province of China.  The outbreak has been 
epidemiologically linked to the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market involving sale of sea food and 
live animals in mid-December, 2019.  Subsequently, the etiological agent was found to be a novel 
corona virus which was isolated from the Broncho alveolar lavage of three infected individuals. 
WHO named the novel coronavirus "Covid -19", "Co" stands for "corona", "vi" for "virus" and "d" 
for "disease", while "19" was for the year, as the outbreak was first identified on December 31 and 
International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) has named the virus as SARS -CoV-2. 
As on 11 th November 2020, g lobally there have been 50,810,763 confirmed cases of COVID -19, 
including 1,263,844 deaths. 
 
1.2 With regard to the origin of the virus, the Secre tary, Department of Health and Family 
Welfare in the Committee's meeting held on 4th August, 2020 submitted the following: 
 
"There are two strands of evidence present ly available in public domain. The first 
group of studies indicate  that it originated from bats. Therefore, the possibility of 
any external factor resulting in mutation in the nature of virus is ruled out.  That is 
the first strand of evidence.  There is another strand of study with some evidence 
which try to argue that there was genetic manipulation and lab engineering leading 
to creation of a particular kind of virus.  But, they are not conclusive.  This is only 
one assessment.  If you look at only the number of Papers in favour of it originating 
out of bats or number of  Papers saying that it was engineered in a lab, the number 
of Papers which favour bat -origin are far more in number when compared to this. 
But, this is an evolving situation.  People are still writing on it and we are closely 
following it." 
 
1.3 As per the  information submitted by the Ministry, all available evidence for COVID -19 
suggests that the causative virus (SARS -CoV-2) has a zoonotic source. Many crucial 
epidemiological parameters like extent and role played by sub -clinical/asymptomatic infections, 
period of communicability etc. still remain under investigation. The infection is spread through 
droplets or prolonged contact with infected patients. Due to the fast spread of virus to neighboring 
countries, it became critical for all countries to expedite  setting up diagnostics for this new virus. 
Diagnosis helps in early identification of the disease and containment of the disease. 
 
1.4 The Coronavirus disease  COVID-19 is a pandemic which has spread its tentacles in more 
than 215 countries. It is caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome Coronavirus 2  (SARS-CoV-
2) that has caused massive panic and public concern across the common masses. Coronaviruses are 
a large family of viruses which are known to cause respiratory infections ranging from the 
common c old to more severe diseases such as Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) and 
Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS). The patients affected with COVID -19 have 
symptoms of fever, cough, breathlessness and other respiratory problem.  
 

2 
 
1.5 The Government of India has adopted inter -sectoral proactive, pre -emptive and graded 
response/policies and priorities by adopting various strategies, the contingent plan during various 
lockdown & unlock phases to combat the COVID -19. The pandemic has forced the world to grasp 
a new normal, with self isolation and social/physical distancing being the global way of life today 
as crucial weapon against the virus.  WHO (under International Health Regulations) has declared 
this outbreak as a “Public Health Emergency of Internat ional Concern” (PHEIC) on 30 th January 
2020 and subsequently declared COVID-19 a pandemic on 11th March, 2020.  
 
Past pandemics and strategies adopted 
 
1.6 India has witnessed widespread illnesses and virus outbreaks in parts of the country, 
including the SARS outbreak between 2002-2004, however, statistics show that since the 1990s, 
they were nowhere as widespread as the COVID -19 that has now reached almost every part of the 
country and almost every country in the world. Prior to outbreak of COVI D-19, most notable viral 
disease outbreaks were Avian influenza (2006-08), H1N1pdm09 Influenza pandemic (2009), Zika 
virus disease (2016-18) and Nipah virus disease (2018, 2019).  
1.7 Avian influenza outbreaks (2006 -08) reported from multiple States (Mahar ashtra, Gujarat, 
Assam, West Bengal etc.) resulted in large number of deaths among poultry. Since then sporadic 
outbreaks are reported mainly due to disease transmitted by the migratory birds. All these 
outbreaks were contained as per the containment plan following One Health approach and in 
coordination with D epartment of Animal Husbandry. Due to prompt containment operations, 
among poultry, no case of avian influenza in humans has been detected in India so far.  
1.8 The Influenza pandemic in 2009 (caused by H1N1pdm09 virus) affected all  parts of the 
country, particularly cities in the States of Maharashtra (Pune, Mumbai), Gujarat (Ahmedabad, 
Surat), Rajasthan (Jaipur, Jodhpur), Delhi, Andhra Pradesh(then) (Hyderabad), Tamil Nadu 
(Chennai), Kerala (Trivandrum, Cochin). In the Influenza pandemic years of 2009-10, there were a 
total of 47840 cases and 2744 deaths reported. Initially , the plan of action involved surveillance at 
points of entry to prevent entry of disease and containment of outbreaks within the community. 
With large outbreaks being reported from these States, a mitigation plan was implemented with 
focus on fatality mitigation. Since then seasonal outbreaks of Influenza A are reported every year. 
Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) is  conducting surveillance for Influenza Like 
Illness (ILI), providing appropriate response and monitoring the outbreak situation.   
1.9 Zika virus disease was declared as a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by 
WHO in February, 2016. In India sporadic cases were reported in 2016 and 2017 from Gujarat 
(Ahmadabad) and Tamil Nadu (Krishnagiri). Large outbreaks were reported in 2018 from Gujarat 
(Ahmadabad), Rajasthan (Jaipur) and Madhya Pradesh (Bhopal, Sehore and Vidisha). Containment 
activities as per the Zika action plan was implemented and all these outbreaks were successfully 
contained. No case has been reported since then.  
1.10 Nipah virus disease outbreaks in 2018 (Kozhikode and Malappuram districts) and 2019 
(Cochin) were localized to thes e districts of the State of Kerala and resulted in 17 deaths 
(laboratory confirmed in 16 deaths; 2018 outbreak)
